posts.title: How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Innovations Across Ads Ranking Models
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Our previous post in this series introduced the Ranking Engineer Agent (REA), an autonomous system that generates hypotheses, designs experiments, and proves new machine learning (ML) techniques on ads ranking models. 
Now, we’re sharing how we propagate ranking model improvements like architectural advancements and training optimizations efficiently across a large and diverse fleet of ads ranking models.  
This post walks through this process that we call “technique propagation” and how we’re optimizing the process using AI agents.
Since agents began driving execution in March 2026, we estimate AI agents handle over 60% of all technique propagation. Measured against the same work before agents, early results show 3x greater engineering productivity, a median 4x reduction in training compute across select combinations, and an estimated $45M+ in compute savings by the end of the year.
Meta’s ads recommendation system is powered by a large number of distinct ads ranking models, each serving different product surfaces and advertiser objectives, and each with its own architecture, training data, and serving constraints. 
Across this portfolio, ML researchers and engineers are continuously advancing the state-of-the-art through innovations we call “techniques.” A technique is anything that makes a ranking model better such as architectural advancements like Wukong factorization layers, Interformer interaction networks, richer data representations, training optimizations, or efficiency improvements in training and inference.
However, because each model has its own architecture, data, and training and serving constraints, a technique proven on one model almost never copy-pastes onto the next. At the same time, speed matters because ML techniques have a shelf life. An innovation that delivers gains today may be superseded within a couple of model development cycles. The faster proven techniques reach the full model fleet, the more value they deliver before the next generation of techniques arrive.
So how do we propagate a technique to a diverse fleet of models as quickly as possible, while minimizing engineering bandwidth and compute? 
Scaling Technique Propagation
Propagating a growing inventory of proven techniques across a large fleet of diverse models creates a combinatorially expanding space of technique-model combinations to explore, where both engineering bandwidth and compute become significant constraints.
The standard way to adapt a technique is to have engineers who are domain experts manually execute adaptation. An engineer studies how a technique interacts with a specific model’s architecture, generalizes it, and tunes it to that model’s constraints. This produces the strongest results, and is still the process for our highest-revenue models, but it does not scale to all of the models in the space. Each adaptation is effort-intensive and demands deep familiarity with both the technique and the target model. So throughput is capped by engineering bandwidth while the opportunity for adaptation grows much faster.
The second constraint on propagation is compute. Every adaptation attempt requires a training run, and with a finite compute budget the question is not only which techniques to try but how to navigate the combinatorial space of configurations without spending the budget on attempts (most of which will produce suboptimal gains). 
Both constraints point to the same requirement: To propagate techniques to a large number of diverse models quickly, propagation has to become standardized, automated, and able to make judgment calls. 
We started by standardizing model design and automating propagation: a template-driven approach organizes models into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, so a technique validated once at the template level propagates automatically to every model built from that template. Over the last 2 years, through standardization and automation, we have shipped 5,000+ technique-model combinations across our large, diverse fleet of models while reducing per-model engineering time by 92%. You can read more about it in our post on Standard Model Templates (SMT).
Standardization and automation handle the deterministic steps, but successful and efficient propagation still requires making judgment calls, such as which technique is worth propagating to which model, how wide a hyperparameter search should be, why a model is not showing gains, or how to detect and resolve failures. Those decisions still required significant human bandwidth, which prevented us from scaling further and from reaching a state where all techniques reached all applicable models within a few weeks of being proven.
That is where AI agents come in.
Scaling Technique Propagation With AI Agents

Our technique propagation system is built around three capabilities:
Discovery: Keep a live view of which techniques have been proven and estimate how well each might transfer to generate a prioritized set of technique-model candidates, ranked by expected impact.
Generalization: Generalize a proven technique so it works on models it was not originally designed for. For models built from shared templates, a technique is generalized once per template and reaches every model built from it. Beyond what templates cover, each model needs its own adaptation, which is where the deepest technical reasoning happens.
Adoption: Turn validated adaptations into shipped models, many at a time: launching experiments, managing asynchronous multi-day training runs, monitoring convergence, diagnosing and recovering from failures, and assembling proposals that can land.
Today, AI agents supercharge all the above capabilities by taking on the judgment-heavy, non-deterministic decision making and bringing deep intelligence to the system. They combine LLM-based reasoning with specialized ML tooling to handle the work of deciding which adaptations to try, diagnosing why something failed and automatically mitigating it, navigating hyperparameter search spaces efficiently, and managing capacity across hundreds of concurrent jobs. The agents share a common knowledge base, an accumulated record of prior training runs, model architectures, and technique outcomes, so they build on what has already been learned rather than starting from scratch.

How Agents Speed Up Discovery
Discovery answers two questions: What proven techniques exist, and how applicable are they to each model in the model fleet? Until recently, domain experts answered both, working through the assessments one model at a time. They tracked research and results across the organization, spotted the techniques worth propagating, and relied on their domain knowledge to judge applicability.
Agents aren’t constrained by the same knowledge or engineering bandwidth limitations as domain experts. Instead of relying on what any one expert knows, they draw on the shared knowledge base, and they make assessments across the entire model fleet at once rather than one model at a time. They systematically identify which proven techniques exist, estimate their transferability across the model fleet, and produce prioritized technique lists ranked by expected impact. Engineers now only have to review the agents’ assessments and make a decision from there.
How Agents Make Generalization More Computationally Efficient 
Generalization is the process of re-implementing a technique proven on one model so it applies to models with different architectures, feature representations, training data, and serving constraints. The core idea usually transfers, but the implementation almost never does. The customization needed depends on the technique and the target model, ranging from retuning hyperparameters, to adapting features to what the target model already consumes or resizing the architecture to fit its inference budget, to redesigning the technique outright. Deciding what a given model needs, and how far to go, is a judgment call.
Depending on whether a model is built from standardized templates or customized individually, generalization comes in two flavors, and agents assist with both:
Template generalization: For models built from standardized templates, agents assist with building, evaluating, and improving the templates themselves. They propose template optimization hypotheses from proven techniques, launch experiments across representative model sets, evaluate results, diagnose failures, and iterate through multiple rounds, helping manage the multi-day loops that template development requires. Validating a technique once at the template level costs a fraction of the compute of adapting each model separately.
Bespoke generalization: For our highest-revenue models, where we still customize a technique for each model, agents progressively learn while working alongside ML engineers during the initial application of a technique to a small number of models. As the engineer makes adaptation decisions such as adjusting configurations, tuning hyperparameters, or resolving failures, the agent tracks every change and outcome, encoding what works, what doesn’t, and which decisions are model-specific versus generalizable. With that grounding, the agent proposes and tests adaptations for the remaining models, with the engineer reviewing and steering rather than driving each one.
Drawing on millions of prior training runs and each target model’s own properties, agents start from the configurations most likely to work, use the results of each round of training runs to narrow the hyperparameter search space for the next, and decide which experiments are worth continuing and which to stop early. As a result, when measured across select technique-model combinations, we have seen a median 4x reduction in training compute.
How Agents Accelerate Adoption
At the adoption stage, agents ship generalized techniques model-by-model. They launch experiments, manage asynchronous multi-day training runs, fine-tune each model, monitor convergence, recover from failures, and assemble validated proposals.
Fine-tuning happens differently depending on how the technique arrived. For techniques applied individually, agents help find the best configuration of technique bundles for that particular model. For models built from a shared template, an auto-research loop searches on top of the template, tuning each model for the gains the shared configuration alone does not deliver.
When failures occur, whether from an infrastructure issue, training divergence, or a data pipeline error, integrated debugging and recovery diagnose the root cause and apply targeted fixes or retries. 
Running hundreds of these workflows at once raises the question of which jobs get priority, and which runs are worth continuing or stopping early. Getting the most out of a fixed compute budget is a global optimization problem, and it is where we are currently investing. Agents monitor concurrent training jobs, rank them by revenue importance, technique potential, and deadline proximity, and reclaim capacity from stalled or low-value runs, so GPUs stay pointed at the highest-value work rather than sitting idle or queued behind lower-priority experiments.
In the past, an engineer had to watch each run, triage every failure by hand, and restart it, which capped each of them at a handful of models. Now they can keep oversight at the decision points, approving plans and setting priorities at a 3x greater productivity (each engineer can now handle 3x more technique-model adaptations), compressing the time from a proven technique to a shipped model.
How We Evaluate Agent-Driven Propagation
Techniques propagated by agents are evaluated the same way as those propagated by engineers. A technique has to show improved offline metrics for predictive performance, such as normalized entropy (NE), while not regressing on key guardrails like training or inference cost. It then has to show a statistically significant win in online A/B testing before it can be shipped.
But a single evaluation at the end comes too late to steer an agent working across stages over days. Each stage produces a different artifact, so each needs its own metrics. This is how we validate what agents are doing.
Discovery: We measure the precision and recall of the technique-model candidates agents select. For a given technique, precision is the share of selected models where the technique ultimately ships, and recall is the share of all viable models for that technique that agents surfaced. Recall matters more here, since a model missed at this stage never gets a second chance; precision acts as a guardrail against spending compute on techniques that will not work.
Generalization: We evaluate techniques generalized by agents across a wide range of models to ensure each delivers gains beyond the model it was originally proven on. We first test every generalized technique on scaled-down versions of models, screening technique-model adaptations broadly while keeping compute usage efficient. Then techniques that pass are evaluated on a representative set of full-size models, where they must improve NE and meet every guardrail metric before moving to adoption.
Adoption: At this stage, we continue to evaluate correctness with the same predictive performance and guardrail metrics as before. But adoption is also the most operationally heavy stage, with experiments that run for days, so we evaluate agent productivity as well. Two metrics matter most: the number of human interventions needed to complete an experiment, which shows how much engineering time each experiment still takes, and the percentage of issues agents diagnose and mitigate on their own.
Humans continue to be key stakeholders throughout the propagation process, reviewing key decisions, confirming judgment calls, and ultimately approving what ships.
Making Agent-Driven Propagation the Standard at Meta 
Given our early results, we are ramping agent-driven workflows to be the primary modality for technique propagation across the model fleet.
Today it can take over a year for every proven technique to reach every applicable model. We’re aiming to reduce that time down to three months. Achieving that means pushing agent-driven workflows toward 5x higher end-to-end throughput, so propagation keeps pace with innovation rather than trailing it. 
To get there we are continuing to invest in the intelligence of the agents themselves, improving the quality of generalization, capacity efficiency, and execution through self-evolving learning, where agents refine their own strategies based on accumulated outcomes rather than relying solely on human-provided heuristics.
Propagating techniques across the models is one component of a larger vision. We are agentifying every aspect of the end-to-end model development lifecycle across the ranking AI space, from exploration and hypothesis generation to propagation, experimentation, and production launch. These agents represent the scaling layer of this system, ensuring that every proven innovation reaches its full potential across the model fleet.

posts.title: Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Building a Template-Driven ML Ecosystem
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
As ML ecosystems grow to a large number of production models, the bottleneck is no longer inventing new techniques to improve these models, but rather shipping them reliably and efficiently across a fragmented model space, creating a rising tide that lifts all the boats.
At Meta, we built a template-driven approach that standardizes model design into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, turning model iteration from a per-model problem into a shared systems problem.
Over the last two years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations, improved offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift covering 70% of models by count.
This work is fully detailed in our paper, “Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems.”
Meta’s ads ranking systems process billions of daily requests across a diverse array of products and optimization goals, served by a large number of production models. At that scale, the main challenge in improving user relevance and advertiser value has shifted from inventing new techniques to propagating them. Every high-impact idea needs to reach every model it applies to, and adapting it one model at a time does not scale with the fleet.
Fragmentation compounds quickly in large-scale ML systems. A new architecture lands on one model, but bringing it to every corner of the ecosystem may take years. A platform migration works for one family of models, but breaks on a long tail of specialized configurations. A tuning insight improves one model, but says little about the next one because the underlying setup is too different. Over time, propagation becomes more difficult than the innovation itself.
Meta’s ads ranking ecosystem ran into this exact problem. As the number of production models grew with the diversity of ads optimization objectives, so did the diversity of architectures, features, training settings, serving constraints, and platform-specific logic. That diversity gave teams flexibility, but it also created three systemic problems: high engineering cost to ship new ideas broadly, high reliability cost from an explosion of corner cases, and low predictability when trying to estimate the ecosystem-wide impact of a change.
The deeper issue is that fragmentation creates an unfavorable scaling law for engineering itself. If each idea must be evaluated and adapted per model, the work grows linearly with the number of models. That is manageable early on, but becomes a serious bottleneck when you have a large number of models. 
Fragmentation also weakens automation. AutoML and optimization systems work best in a structured space, but when every model has a different shape, the highest-potential techniques reach only a subset of models.
Our answer was not to add another layer of automation on top of this complexity. Instead, we started by reducing the complexity itself. We did this by introducing Standard Model Templates (SMT), an approach that standardizes model design into a curated set of reusable templates.
Figure 1: Before SMT, each technique was tuned by hand on each model, and the combinations to try grew exponentially. With SMT, multi-model optimization tunes techniques once across representative models, and the ones that generalize go into the next template version.
A Template-Driven Foundation
A template is an opinionated, minimal model setup built from shared components such as architecture choices, feature logic, training settings, and serving configs. Instead of maintaining every production model as a largely independent design, we group similar models around a smaller number of standard templates. Model-specific logic still exists where necessary, but the common parts are explicitly represented and shared.
In practice, we use a small set of templates that cover major ranking and retrieval patterns across different model sizes. These templates package reusable components for feature selection, feature interaction, model parallelism, training configuration, and hardware-aware serving.
This changes the operating model in an important way. Instead of evaluating a new idea independently on every model, we can evaluate it on a much smaller set of representative templates and then propagate it to the model groups that use them. In other words, we shift from per-model iteration to template-level iteration.
That gives us three main advantages.
Reduced propagation complexity: A shared template lets one implementation serve many downstream models, which lowers the cost of shipping new ideas at scale.
Improved reliability: When there are fewer unique model setups, it becomes practical to build stronger validation, better guardrails, and more transferable debugging workflows. Problems such as training instability or serving regressions become easier to reason about because they occur within a shared template structure rather than an unbounded configuration space.
Improved predictability: When models in a group share a common template, performance on representative models becomes a much better signal for the rest of the group. That makes ecosystem-level planning more grounded and less assumption-driven.
Over time, this template-driven approach became more than a standardization effort. It became the foundation for a broader ML development system.
Figure 2: The SMT development loop (left) and the layered architecture inside each template (right). Techniques are tuned once across representative models, added to a new template version, and rolled out to every model built on it.
SMTs: From Standardization to Scalable Technique Transfer
The shift to SMTs unlocked a more ambitious capability — the ability to optimize the entire ecosystem as a single, cohesive unit. Rather than managing a fleet of independent models, we began treating the landscape as a shared innovation surface.
Instead of propagating individual techniques one by one, we transfer proven holistic model designs from strong source models into target model families through a shared template layer. This matters because many gains come from interactions between architectural choices, scaling decisions, and training strategies, not from isolated components applied independently.
Over the last 2 years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations across our large diverse fleet of models , while improving offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift. More importantly, it challenged a common assumption that diverse optimization goals require highly diversified model designs. In many cases, a well-designed shared template can generalize much further than expected.
We also found that once model structure is standardized, scaling decisions become more reusable. Rather than rediscovering cost-performance trade-offs separately for every model, we can learn them in template space and apply them more broadly. This led to scaling-law-based optimization workflows that make resource allocation more principled and less ad hoc.
Multi-Model Optimization
We use multi-model optimization to make template iteration rigorous. This process evaluates candidate techniques across representative models and searches for configurations that improve aggregate performance while limiting regressions.
A technique with a strong average gain but frequent regressions is difficult to ship across a large fleet. Consistency is as important as peak improvement for production-scale propagation. Multi-model optimization considers both aggregate performance and regression rate when deciding whether a technique is ready for integration.
After optimization, candidate techniques are validated on held-out models to check whether gains transfer beyond the representative set. Techniques that pass are integrated into the next template version. Over the last two years, we shipped 80 new ML techniques through this workflow.
The result is compounding. Every model that adopts a mature template inherits a history of generalized improvements rather than starting from an isolated baseline.
Why SMT Matters for Agentic ML Systems
Agentic model building often envisions a single end-to-end agent exploring a large design space with access to tools, training pipelines, and evaluation results. In practice, that approach runs into a familiar problem: The search space is too unconstrained. Without strong priors, an agent spends too much effort exploring unproductive regions, recovering from avoidable failures, or proposing changes that are difficult to explain and harder to ship.
SMT helps solve that problem because they encode known-good design patterns, which gives agents a structured starting point, a bounded search space, and a quality floor. Instead of treating model building as free-form search, we can decompose it into specialized subproblems.
At Meta, SMTs are also the foundation for our multi-agent approach to model building. Templates provide the structure, and agents provide adaptive exploration and automation. At the template level, agents help build, evaluate, and improve the templates themselves. They propose optimization ideas based on proven techniques, launch experiments across representative models, diagnose failures, and iterate over multiple rounds, which helps manage the multi-day loops that template development requires. Agents can also take on harder work such as migrating models to new hardware platforms. A technique validated this way reaches every model built from that template, at a fraction of the compute it would take to adapt each model separately. We cover this in more detail in our post, How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Techniques Across Ads Ranking Models.
Lessons Learned and the Road Ahead for SMTs
Propagating ML innovations to improve models is often the main scaling challenge in large ML ecosystems. SMTs succeed because automation gets more powerful as the underlying system becomes more structured. Template-driven development did not just make the ecosystem easier for humans to operate. It also made it easier for optimization systems, scaling workflows, and agents to reason effectively.
But standardization only works if it is opinionated enough to remove unnecessary diversity, while still preserving the limited flexibility that matters. A template system that tries to accommodate every historical edge case will eventually recreate the fragmentation it was meant to solve.
There is more work to do in improving template coverage, strengthening scaling-law-based optimization, and moving toward fully end-to-end agentic workflows — including agentic template building, model generation, online evaluation, and continuous optimization from online signals. We also need to make these workflows more reliable and more explainable.
But the central idea has held up. If you want to scale ML innovation across a large ecosystem, you need to standardize the surface on which that innovation lands. In other words, designing once and deploying at scale is not just an efficiency tactic; it is an architectural choice about how to make a large ML ecosystem learn faster.
Read the Paper
“Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems.”

posts.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability: Update Your JetBrains IDEs, ReSharper, .NET Tools, Toolbox App, and Gateway Now
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Summary
A critical security issue named Java4Shell was identified in OpenJDK, the basis of JetBrains Runtime (JBR), which is bundled with all JetBrains IDEs, ReSharper, the JetBrains Toolbox App, and Gateway.
The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and presents the weakness CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).
If abused, the flaw may enable an attacker to crash the IDE or, in the worst case, execute code remotely on your machine. 
Only IDEs running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support are exposed. ARM64, including Apple Silicon, is not affected.
The IDE updates listed below mitigate the issue for every supported release line. We encourage all users to update to the latest versions.
If you cannot update yet, a one-line VM option removes the exposure.
You must update the Java runtimes that your projects use for builds, tests, and run configurations separately, as they are not covered by IDE updates.
Details
On November 17, 2026, Oracle and the OpenJDK project released fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM. The issue was reported by Calif and is known as Java4Shell. 
To decode Base64 faster, HotSpot uses an intrinsic routine on x86-64 CPUs that support AVX-512 VBMI. Malformed input makes this routine write past the end of a Java array and corrupt neighboring memory. The reporters demonstrated how this routine could be exploited to execute arbitrary code in several server-side Java applications. OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, along with the 21, 25, and 27 lines, are affected across Java distributions. Oracle’s Java SE 8 Performance Pack (8u511-perf and earlier) is also affected, while standard Java 8 and Java 11 builds are not.
Every JetBrains IDE bundles JetBrains Runtime, which is based on OpenJDK. All current releases that bundle JBR 17 (17.0.6 and later), 21, or 25 are affected. This includes IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, GoLand, Rider, CLion, RubyMine, RustRover, DataGrip, and the JetBrains HTTP Client CLI, as well as remote development backends.
An IDE is exposed only if both of the following conditions are true: It runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, such as Intel Xeon processors from Ice Lake onward, some tenth- and eleventh-generation Intel Core processors, or AMD processors based on Zen 4 or newer; and it decodes Base64 data controlled by an attacker, for example, data received from a network peer.
At the time of publication, we are not aware of this vulnerability having been exploited against JetBrains IDEs.
The updates listed below mitigate the issue by adding the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics option to the default VM options of all JetBrains IDEs. The option turns off the vulnerable routine for every use of java.util.Base64 in the IDE process. Base64 decoding then falls back to the regular Java implementation, which may be slower. The option is accepted on every platform. The upstream fix is being integrated into JetBrains Runtime separately, and we will update this post when new runtime builds are available.
The mitigation is included in the following IDE versions:

IDE2026.32026.22026.12025.32025.2
CLion2026.3.0.22026.2.5.12026.1.5.32025.3.6.42025.2.6.4
DataGrip2026.3.0.12026.2.7.12026.1.4.22025.3.6.22025.2.6.2
DataSpell——2026.1.3.22025.3.3.22025.2.4.2
Gateway2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.4.12025.3.3.12025.2.6.1
GoLand2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.5.32025.2.6.4
IntelliJ IDEA2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.5
PhpStorm2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4
PyCharm2026.3.0.22026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4
Rider2026.3.0.22026.2.5.12026.1.5.42025.3.6.42025.2.6.3
RubyMine2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4
RustRover2026.3.1.12026.2.6.12026.1.4.22025.3.7.22025.2.6.2
WebStorm2026.3.0.12026.2.5.12026.1.5.22025.3.6.32025.2.6.4





Toolbox App needs to be updated to 3.9.2.
ReSharper needs to be updated to one of the following versions: 2026.3.0.2, 2026.2.5.1, 2026.1.5.4, 2025.3.5.4, or 2025.2.6.3.
How to protect yourself
Update your IDE. Download the latest version of your IDE from the JetBrains website or use the automatic update option in the Toolbox App or in Help | Check for Updates.
If you cannot update yet, apply the workaround. Open Help | Edit Custom VM Options, add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics on a new line, save the file, and restart the IDE. Do not use -XX:UseAVX=2 with JetBrains IDEs, even though some public advisories suggest it, as doing so will prevent JBR 25 from starting on ARM64.
Update the Java runtimes used by your projects. The IDE update only covers the IDE process. Build and run processes that use a project JDK, such as Gradle and Maven daemons, tests, and run configurations, are not covered. Update those JDKs to your vendor’s fixed build, for example, Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1. Other vendors, including Eclipse Temurin and Amazon Corretto, use their own build numbers, so check the vendor advisory. Until you can update, you can start those JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a workaround.
Check your exposure and confirm the option is active. If you use Linux, you can see whether your CPU supports AVX-512 VMBI by following the instructions in the Affected products section of the Calif write-up. To confirm that a running IDE uses the option, run jcmd <pid> VM.flags. This is useful if you maintain a custom VM options file or run a remote development backend.
The IDE updates and the workaround address only the vulnerability described above. We always recommend using the latest IDE version to benefit from other security updates.
For the upstream advisories and the write-up from the reporters, see:
OpenJDK Vulnerability Advisory: 2026/11/17
Oracle Critical Security Patch Update Advisory – November 2026
Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere by Calif
A complete list of recently fixed security issues is available on the Fixed security issues page on the JetBrains website. You can also subscribe to receive notifications about fixes in all JetBrains products via email.
Frequently asked questions
Which versions are affected?
All JetBrains IDE versions that bundle JBR 17 (17.0.6 and later), 21, or 25 are affected until they are updated to the versions listed above, or until the workaround is applied. An IDE is exposed only on x86-64 hardware with AVX-512 VBMI. We recommend upgrading as soon as possible.
Is it possible to backport the fix to other versions?
We are not considering backports to older IDE versions. The workaround described above prevents this issue and is compatible with them.
I use remote development. What should I do?
The remote IDE backend is an IDE process and receives the same default VM options as desktop IDE builds with the update. Remote hosts are often cloud x86-64 machines that support AVX-512 VBMI, so be sure to update the backend, or add the option to its custom VM options in the meantime.
I already added the option manually. Do I need to remove it once I update to a new version?
No. After you update, the option is one of the default VM options, so the manual entry is redundant but harmless. We will remove the default option once the IDEs bundle a version of JetBrains Runtime that contains the upstream fix.
Support
If you have any questions regarding this issue or encounter problems updating, please get in touch with the JetBrains Support team by submitting a ticket.

posts.title: Kotlin Benchmark 2.0: How AI Coding Agents Handle Harder Tasks and Closed-Source Code
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
In July, we released the Kotlin Benchmark – a collection of 105 real repository-level tasks for evaluating AI coding agents’ work with Kotlin. Since then, we’ve updated it to be more representative of what Kotlin teams do, with more reliable results and more data to help you choose an agent-model configuration.
The new tasks require changes across multiple files, come from projects in different Kotlin domains, and include code from private repositories. To prevent reward hacking and improve the reliability of our results, we restricted network access when agents solve open-source tasks, so they can’t look up a fix that has already been published. We also set  30-minute-per-task resolution time limit for each configuration, balancing the additional time required to solve complex problems with the need for a manageable evaluation time.
See the latest Kotlin Benchmark results
What’s new 





Harder tasks: The collection of tasks now focuses on medium- and high-complexity problems that require multi-step reasoning, debugging, and changes across multiple files. Simple single-file edits have been filtered out.
Open-source and closed-source tasks: Of the 100 tasks, 70 come from open-source GitHub repositories and 30 from private JetBrains ones, where neither the code nor the fix is available online. The leaderboard shows the results for the full suite and for each group separately, allowing for a direct comparison of the configuration’s performance on public and private code.
Broader Kotlin domain coverage: The 70 open-source tasks now come from 25 repositories, and they span key Kotlin domains: 30 Android, 20 backend, 10 Kotlin Multiplatform, and 10 libraries and tools. The 30 closed-source tasks come from internal JetBrains server-side Kotlin projects.
Restricted network access to prevent reward hacking: Agents complete the open-source tasks without network access, so a configuration can’t inflate its score by looking up the published fix.
New models, including open ones: The evaluated lineup has changed and now includes open models – Kimi and DeepSeek, both running via OpenCode. If you’re considering an open model, you can compare it with closed ones on the same tasks. Every configuration runs the full suite three times, and the exact agent-model pairings, versions, and run settings are on the leaderboard.
Average cost, tokens, and steps per task: The leaderboard now displays the average cost, tokens, and number of steps per task, alongside resolution rate and latency, so you can see how resource-intensive each configuration is.
Stricter guardrails to prevent solution lookup
When benchmark tasks come from previously solved public issues, an agent can retrieve the existing fix instead of deriving one from the task and the codebase. This is known as reward hacking, and in our preliminary runs, we found agents were doing exactly that.
To prevent it, agents now solve the open-source tasks in a stricter sandbox with restricted network access. Only calls to the model itself are allowed as traffic. Dependencies are cached in advance, the repository history is hidden, and agents are explicitly informed that network access is disabled to prevent repeated attempts to access it. Network access remains available for solving closed-source tasks, because their fixes aren’t published anywhere.
These controls prevent agents from looking up solutions at runtime, but they don’t help rule out data contamination. The open-source repositories and their associated fixes may be part of a model’s training data. That’s the reason for the 30 closed-source tasks, which stay private. The methodology documents the evaluation setup and its limits.
The results
In the new evaluation, the best resolution rate on the full suite (combining both open- and closed-source tasks) comes from Claude Code with Opus 5.5, which posted a 75.3% resolution rate and an average cost of \$0.84 per task. The other 12 configurations resolved between 54.3% and 73.7% and cost between \$0.02 and \$3.14 per task.
For the open-source dataset, the highest-scoring configurations are Claude Code with Fable 5.1 (86.2%), followed by Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (84.8%) and Junie using Opus 5.5 and GPT 6 Luna (79.5%). However, the latter configurations offer a comparable score at lower average costs per task (\$0.68 and \$0.33, respectively, versus \$2.38).
On the closed dataset (consisting of Kotlin server-side tasks), Antigravity CLI with Gemini 3.8 Flash performed the best (60%, \$1.74 per task), closely followed by OpenCode with Deepseek V4.1 Flash (58.9%), which had a more moderate price tag of \$0.08 per task.
As you compare, keep in mind that the latest Kotlin Benchmark uses a different, harder task suite, so its scores are not comparable with the first release. A lower number here doesn’t mean a model got worse. Compare configurations within the same benchmark version.




Results shown here reflect the second public iteration of the Kotlin Benchmark. The leaderboard will be updated as newer model evaluations are added.
As before, a task counts as completed only when the generated patch passes the required tests, and the scores are a comparison signal, not a guarantee for every codebase. Use the leaderboard to shortlist configurations, and then validate them on representative tasks from your own projects.
What’s next
In the coming weeks, we plan to release follow-up materials for this benchmark iteration. Specifically, we will:
Analyze the agentic solutions for the open-source tasks and identify any that have potentially been contaminated (reproduced from memory).
Compile results that go beyond resolution rate: we will run Qodana, the static analysis tool from JetBrains, to determine whether agents introduced any bugs, security issues, or code smells with their solutions. 
The Kotlin Benchmark and the follow-up analyses are part of our own research on how agents work with Kotlin code. By studying how they complete these tasks and where they fail, we learn what to improve in Kotlin and its tooling.
If you’d like to help us improve Kotlin’s compatibility with AI tools, let us know where you run into trouble and use this form to share examples of where AI gives you a poor, incorrect, or unhelpful result when working with Kotlin.
To learn more, explore the leaderboard, read the methodology, or inspect the public tasks and harnesses on GitHub.
Further reading
The Kotlin Benchmark Leaderboard
The Kotlin Benchmark Methodology
Introducing the Kotlin Benchmark for AI Coding Agents

posts.title: Creating Polars Expression Plugins in PyCharm: A Step-by-Step Guide for Rust Beginners
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Polars is a favorite among data scientists. It’s a high-performance, columnar DataFrame library written in Rust and powered by Apache Arrow. 
Unlike traditional single-threaded tools, Polars uses full multicore CPU parallelism, efficient memory allocation, and lazy execution with query optimization. These features let data professionals execute complex joins, filters, and aggregations on large datasets significantly faster while saving RAM.
However, real-world data processing often requires specialized processes to prepare raw data for operational or analytical use cases.
Built-in Polars expressions may not cover highly specialized algorithms or proprietary business logic out of the box. Without custom expression plugins, data engineers and scientists often resort to standard user-defined Python functions or iterative processing. This potentially introduces performance bottlenecks and sacrifices some of Polars’ native speed and memory efficiency. To overcome these bottlenecks, you may want to consider creating Polars expression plugins. 
Polars expression plugins
Polars expression plugins allow you to create custom functions and register them as expressions in the Polars library. The Polars engine dynamically links these functions to the runtime, and their performance will be close to that of native expressions.
Expression plugins offer three key benefits:
Optimization: Plugins seamlessly integrate into Polars’ lazy query engine, allowing expressions to benefit from logical plan optimizations and predicate pushdown.
Parallelism: Expressions automatically leverage Polars’ multi-threaded execution framework to process data chunks concurrently across available CPU cores.
Native performance: Implemented directly in Rust, plugins execute with bare-metal speed and zero Python GIL overhead during runtime.




But there’s a catch: These functions must be implemented in Rust (because of the native functionalities mentioned above). To write Rust code in PyCharm, you will need to install the Rust plugin and configure the Rust toolchain.
The Expression Plugins chapter of the Polars user guide gives you a quick overview of the core concepts. This blog post digs a little deeper and is geared toward PyCharm users who are new to Rust.
Create a Polars plugin project using a template
The Rust plugin in PyCharm uses cargo-generate under the hood, allowing developers to quickly scaffold new Rust projects directly from templates.
To create a Rust project, start by installing the Rust plugin and toolchain, following the instructions in this documentation. Then, while you have the New Project window open, click on the + icon at the bottom.




In this example, we’ll create our Polars plugin from a template I made earlier. Simply paste the URL for this template into the Template URL field and click Add.




Now the template will be available as an option, and we’ll select it for our current project. Don’t forget to use the Location field to establish a location and name for your project. In this example, ours will be called “polars-plugin-demo”.




When we click Create, a project is created with the necessary .toml files and file structure. Then we can just dive straight into it.




Before we start developing, we’ll have to add a Python environment and interpreter, as you can see <No interpreters> in the bottom right of the screenshot above. Let’s set one up now by clicking on <No interpreters> and selecting Add New Interpreter, then Add Local Interpreter. For this example, we’ll use uv (which I’ve already installed). We should also make sure to select the latest Python version, which is Python 3.14 at the time of writing.




With everything set up, we can start creating our custom Polars plugin.
What’s in a Polars plugin project
Let’s start by looking at what’s inside a new project by default
First, we have two .toml files for the project settings. Cargo.toml is for Rust, and pyproject.toml is for Python. Since our project uses both languages, we’ll need both files:
Cargo.toml – Rust dependencies: polars, pyo3, pyo3-polars, and serde.
pyproject.toml – maturin build settings, with module-name wired to polars_plugin_demo._internal.
Now we’ll follow the steps laid out in the Writing the expression section of the Polars user guide. The source code for Rust will be in the src/ folder. This is the same as using maturin init or cargo init to start a Rust project:
src/lib.rs – The _internal PyO3 module and the Polars global allocator.
src/expressions.rs – Empty for now, but your #[polars_expr] functions will go here.
Then we’ll have a directory with the same name as our project. This is where all the Python-specific files are located:
polars_plugin_demo/__init__.py – Where you register each expression with Polars.
polars_plugin_demo/_typing.py – IntoExpr / IntoExprColumn aliases, so we never have to import the private polars._typing.
polars_plugin_demo/_internal.pyi – Type stub for the compiled module.
As we go along, I’ll explain the contents of each file and how they all work together.
If you’re using PyCharm, you might also notice the target/ folder in your project files.  Although we have not built the project yet, once we’ve configured a local virtual environment (.venv) as its Python interpreter, PyCharm regularly scans and indexes the environment. When PyCharm runs background tasks, it can inadvertently trigger PEP 517 build hooks using information in pyproject.toml. However, this build (the target/ folder) is mainly used to service PyCharm’s checking and indexing functionality. We will ignore it for now.
Writing a Polars plugin
Working out the expression logic
As explained above, we will mainly be working in src/expressions.rs, which is currently empty. In our example project, we’ll start by adding this code to the file:
use polars::prelude::*;

use pyo3_polars::derive::polars_expr;

use std::fmt::Write;

fn capitalize_str(value: &str, output: &mut String) {

    if let Some(mut first_char) = value.chars().next() {

        first_char.make_ascii_uppercase();

        write!(output, "{first_char}{}", &value[1..]).unwrap();

    }

}

#[polars_expr(output_type=String)]

fn capitalize(inputs: &[Series]) -> PolarsResult<Series> {

    let ca = inputs[0].str()?;

    let out: StringChunked = ca.apply_into_string_amortized(capitalize_str);

    Ok(out.into_series())

}
Let’s look at this code line by line to understand what it does. First we have the imports:
use polars::prelude::*; – This line brings commonly used Polars types, traits, and macros into scope so they can be used everywhere in the file without specification of their full paths. 
use pyo3_polars::derive::polars_expr; – This line imports the #[polars_expr] attribute macro that we’ll be using. This macro turns an ordinary Rust function into a plugin entry point that Polars can find at runtime.
use std::fmt::Write; – This line is here to ensure that the write!(output, …) macro works properly.




The logic of our expression is implemented in the capitalize_str function. Instead of returning a String, the function takes the input value and a mutable output buffer. This is necessary because it’s the format demanded by apply_into_string_amortized, which we will call later, so that it can promise one allocation for a whole column instead of one per row. 
In this case, the caller in Polars owns the buffer and hands the same one back on every row. Our function can’t own that buffer, because otherwise it only lives for one call. The only way to reuse it is for the caller to hold it and lend it out as a &mut String.
Inside the function:
if let Some(mut first_char) = value.chars().next() {...} provides an owned, mutable copy of the first char as first_char. There’s no mutable borrowing of value itself.  
first_char.make_ascii_uppercase(); capitalizes in place, but only for a–z. Non-ASCII characters are left untouched by design. 
write!(output, "{first_char}{}", &value[1..]).unwrap(); appends the capitalized character plus the rest of the string.




Note that, in this example, we assume that each character is stored in a single byte only. If the first character is multibyte, byte 1 lands mid-character, the slice panics, and the program will stop working.
After the logic is set, the capitalize function with the #[polars_expr] attribute is responsible for exporting the expression. 
#[polars_expr(output_type=String)] – The #[polars_expr] attribute wraps the capitalize function into an extern “C” symbol in the compiled cdylib, plus a companion function reporting the output dtype. output_type=String declares a fixed output schema, so Polars knows the resulting dtype during lazy planning without running anything. 




Note that Polars looks up symbols by name at runtime, which means there’s no need to register our expressions to the module in lib.rs by hand. Instead, we’ll register them on the Python side later.
fn capitalize(inputs: &[Series]) -> PolarsResult<Series> {...} – Every plugin expression has the same signature: It receives its input columns as a slice of Series values and returns a PolarsResult<Series> containing the resulting column or an error.
let ca = inputs[0].str()?; – inputs[0] is the single input column; .str() downcasts the type-erased Series to a &StringChunked (Polars’ typed chunked array). It returns a PolarsResult, so `?` turns an incorrect dtype into a clean Polars error instead of causing a panic that would stop the program.
let out: StringChunked = ca.apply_into_string_amortized(capitalize_str); – out will be a StringChunked type result from moving through the column and calling capitalize_str(value, &mut buf) for each row. As mentioned before, in this process, Polars reuses one String buffer across all rows and copies the bytes into the output Arrow buffer.
Ok(out.into_series()) – At the end, we convert the typed StringChunked back to a Series and wrap it into the Result type’s Ok variant.
Putting it together as a module
Now that we’ve created the expression logic and registered it as a symbol, we can look at the rest of the project and see how the pieces fit together. Let’s look at src/lib.rs, which is the crate root for a Polars expression plugin:
mod expressions;

use pyo3_polars::PolarsAllocator;

/// Polars plugin expressions implemented in Rust.

#[pyo3::pymodule]

mod _internal {

   use pyo3::prelude::*;

   #[pymodule_init]

   fn init(m: &Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {

       m.add("__version__", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))

   }

}

#[global_allocator]

static ALLOC: PolarsAllocator = PolarsAllocator::new();
This code is pure scaffolding, with no expression logic of its own. However, it’s still essential that we understand what it does:
mod expressions; pulls in src/expressions.rs, where your #[polars_expr(...)] functions live. It’s declared here purely so the module gets compiled; nothing in lib.rs calls into it. As mentioned before, the symbols were looked up by name at call time, so there’s no registration list anywhere in this file.
#[pyo3::pymodule]
mod _internal {...} declares the Python extension module using PyO3’s declarative module syntax. The name _internal has to match module-name in pyproject.toml, which is what maturin uses to decide where to drop the compiled _internal.abi3.so inside the Python package.
The module body is nearly empty. But this is intentional, as Polars plugin functions aren’t exposed as Python functions. The only thing #[pymodule_init] does is set __version__ on the module from CARGO_PKG_VERSION, resolved at compile time by env!. The module still matters even though it’s empty because importing it is what loads the .so file into the process, which is what makes the exported #[polars_expr] symbols available for Polars to resolve.
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: PolarsAllocator = PolarsAllocator::new(); installs Polars’ allocator as the Rust-side global allocator. This is the recommended setup for pyo3-polars plugins: It ensures the plugin shares the same allocator as the Polars build it’s loaded next to, keeping memory management compatible when data passes between Polars and the plugin, and it lets Polars’ memory accounting see the plugin’s allocations.
The Python-side setup
Now let’s look at the Python side. There are three files inside the polars_plugin_demo/ folder. These files are all scaffolding for a Polars expression plugin and are essential when adding our custom expressions to Polars.
_typing.py is created because we need a type alias for polars._typing, which is a private module that is subject to change from one release to the next.
__init__.py is where the Python-side registration surface lives. PLUGIN_PATH points to the package directory, where maturin develop drops _internal.abi3.so. The commented-out capitalize demonstrates how one Python wrapper calls register_plugin_function for each #[polars_expr] in src/expressions.rs. function_name needs to match the Rust function name exactly so Polars can locate the correct plugin function.
_internal.pyi is the stub for the compiled extension. However, expression functions are exported as C symbols, not Python attributes, so they do not appear here. We use this file to declare __version__: str.
After reading through these files, uncomment the example in __init__.py:
def capitalize(expr: IntoExpr) -> pl.Expr:

    """Capitalize String."""

    return register_plugin_function(

        plugin_path=PLUGIN_PATH,

        function_name="capitalize",

        args=expr,

        is_elementwise=True,

    )
We are now ready to build our custom Polars expression.
Building and testing our plugin
Although we can build the plugin manually with maturin develop, PyCharm can handle this step for you. It invokes maturin develop to compile your Rust modules into a native shared library (an .so file in this case) and drops it into the designated directory.
Since we’ve configured
[tool.maturin]
module-name = "polars_plugin_demo._internal"
in the pyproject.toml file, our .so file is placed in the polars_plugin_demo/ folder. We also need to make sure the name of the PyO3 module in src/lib.rs matches the last part of module-name (_internal in this case).
To trigger a build, simply run or debut a Python script that uses the plugin. In a real project, you’d typically have a set of Python tests sitting in a tests/ folder or something similar. However, since this is only a demo, let’s keep things simple and use the following script:
import polars as pl

from polars_plugin_demo import capitalize

df = pl.DataFrame(

   {

       "attendees": ["john", "mary", "connor", "sally"],

   }

)

out = df.with_columns(names=capitalize("attendees"))

print(out)
Now that our customized plugin capitalize has been built and included in the polars_plugin_demo module, we can import it and use it like other Polars expressions.
Run the script just like you’d normally do in PyCharm – for example, by clicking the Run button in the top-right corner:




You’ll see the loading bar at the bottom:




This indicates that maturin develop is running in the background. The result is cached, so the next time you run the script (assuming you haven’t made changes to the module), it will execute much faster.
Want a challenge? Try writing some unit tests and running them with pytest to see if everything works as expected.
What’s next?
If you’d like to learn more about how to create Polars plugins, check out my workshop on GitHub. You might also enjoy this tutorial by Marco Gorelli or the Expression Plugins section of the Polars user guide.

Explore more of what the Rust plugin in PyCharm offers to streamline your project with Rust and Python. The plugin enhances cross-language development with intelligent code completion, seamless navigation between Rust and Python modules, and automated refactoring across your codebase. Furthermore, its integrated debugging support lets you step through both Python scripts and compiled Rust code effortlessly, ensuring a smooth and unified workflow.

posts.title: Best GitHub Actions Alternatives in 2026: What 838 Organizations Actually Use
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
GitHub Actions is the default CI/CD tool for much of the industry, because it’s built into GitHub. But 2026 gave teams reasons to look around. 
On July 9, hosted runner jobs were delayed or failing for more than nine hours. In May, the Megalodon campaign pushed malicious workflows to more than 5,500 repositories in one afternoon. And GitHub announced a fee for self-hosted runners, then postponed it after a backlash.
Most GitHub Actions alternatives articles answer with a ranked list of tools. We asked 838 organizations which CI/CD tools they actually use and why. We also counted every Actions incident in GitHub’s availability reports for 2026 and followed what developers say about Actions in public discussions.
The data shows that alternative can mean 4 different things, from changing one line of YAML to leaving GitHub entirely. And the most common choice isn’t a replacement at all: 63% of organizations that use GitHub Actions already run a second CI/CD tool next to it.
Quick picks
Faster, cheaper runners for existing workflows: third-party runner providers.
A second CI for the builds Actions struggles with: TeamCity, for complex build chains, on-prem and special hardware, and predictable costs. Your code stays on GitHub.
Replacing Actions while keeping your code on GitHub: TeamCity, CircleCI, Buildkite, or Jenkins.
Leaving GitHub altogether: GitLab CI/CD, Azure DevOps, or Forgejo / Gitea Actions.
Full disclosure: we make TeamCity. We say where it fits, and where it doesn’t.
Key findings
Teams choose Actions because they’re already on GitHub. Only 7 of 204 respondents mentioned price.
Most teams add a tool rather than replace one. 63% of Actions organizations also run another CI/CD tool, and 66% of Actions-first teams have no plans to switch.
Faster runners fix only part of the problem. Teams that consider leaving Actions name cost and performance (30% each), but also stability (26%) and debugging (19%), which a runner swap doesn’t fix (n=43, directional).
Outages are a monthly event. GitHub reported 21 incidents affecting Actions in January–October 2026, about 70 hours in total.
Actions is easy to start with but harder to trust. 69% of Actions-first teams are satisfied with its ease of use, but reliability is the aspect they’re most often dissatisfied with (22.5%).

Why teams keep GitHub Actions
We asked organizations whose primary tool is Actions why they adopted it (204 answers). Most came down to one thing:
“It’s there. Built into github.”
That’s a real strength: no setup, native PR checks, a huge marketplace. But it also means Actions is weakest where your needs go beyond a GitHub repository: specific hardware, on-prem networks, other version control systems, or complex build graphs. 
That’s why only 37% of Actions organizations use it as their only CI/CD tool.

CI/CD Tools Adoption Survey 2026, 158 open-ended answers grouped into themes. One answer can belong to several themes.

The most common reasons for a second tool are legacy systems, unfinished migrations, client requirements, and teams with different needs. A frequent pattern: “Internal projects are maintained in gitlab / use gitlab ci, public / oss products use GitHub / gh actions.” 
Organizations that have Actions but chose another tool as primary most often cite self-hosting and on-premises requirements.
Where GitHub Actions falls short
Read any long developer discussion about GitHub Actions, on Reddit or in GitHub’s own community forum, and the same complaints keep coming up:
Pricing and billing, especially since GitHub announced a fee for self-hosted runners.
Speed and caching: slow builds and caches that are hard to control.
Self-hosted runner operations: keeping your own runners patched, scaled, and healthy.
YAML and workflow complexity, and how hard it is to debug a workflow or run it locally.
Outages of the Actions service itself.
Permissions, secrets, and supply-chain risk from third-party marketplace actions.
Vendor lock-in: workflows that only run on GitHub.
Our survey puts numbers on part of this. We asked 227 teams whose main CI/CD tool is Actions how satisfied they are with 11 aspects of it. Actions scores best on ease of use (69% satisfied) and setup (63%). Dissatisfaction is highest for reliability (22.5%), user interface (21.6%), logs and error messages (21.5%), and performance (20.7%). The survey didn’t ask about security, so supply-chain risk isn’t covered by these numbers.

Pricing and self-hosted runners
The loudest recent debate was about GitHub’s December 2025 plan to charge $0.002 per minute for self-hosted runners, which GitHub postponed with no new date. Self-hosted runners are still free, but the lesson stuck: on Actions, CI costs are tied to minutes, and someone else sets the price of a minute.
Speed and debugging
Performance and logs are two of the four aspects Actions users are least happy with. Debugging is the hard part: you can’t easily rerun a job interactively or run a workflow locally without third-party tools.

That’s 21 of the 57 major incidents GitHub reported, about 70 hours of degraded Actions service. 14 lasted two hours or more. July was the worst month, including the 9-hour runner provisioning failure.
Supply-chain security
On March 19, 2026, attackers force-pushed 76 of 77 tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action, a popular security-scanning action. Every workflow that referenced it by a version tag ran code that stole CI credentials. In May, the Megalodon campaign pushed secret-stealing workflows to 5,561 repositories.
Both attacks exploit the same thing: most Actions workflows run third-party code from the marketplace, referenced by tags that can be moved to point at different code. The marketplace makes Actions fast to adopt, and it’s also its biggest attack surface.
Path 1: Swap the runners
Providers such as Blacksmith, Depot, RunsOn, Namespace, WarpBuild, and Ubicloud run your existing Actions jobs on their own machines or in your cloud account. You change one line per job:
 jobs:
   build:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: <provider-runner-label>
GitHub charges $0.006 per minute for a standard 2-vCPU Linux runner. Most providers list the same machine at $0.001–$0.004; some match GitHub’s price and compete on speed instead. (Prices checked on November 19, 2026.) The market moves fast: BuildJet shut down in March 2026.
What it doesn’t fix: your workflows still run on Actions, so YAML, debugging, permissions, marketplace risk, and control-plane outages stay the same. In our survey, teams that consider leaving Actions name cost and performance most often, but stability and debugging come right after, and a runner swap doesn’t touch those.

Choose this path if your only complaints are build time and cost.
Path 2: Add a second CI next to Actions
This is what most organizations do. Actions keeps linting and PR checks; heavy or special workloads move to a tool that handles them better: release builds, long test suites, hardware-bound jobs, on-prem deployments, or code outside GitHub. The most common second tools are Jenkins (25% of Actions organizations), GitLab CI (22%), Azure DevOps (14%), AWS CodePipeline / CodeBuild (11%), and TeamCity (7%).
TeamCity
TeamCity is a CI/CD server from JetBrains, available on-premises or in the cloud. It builds your GitHub pull requests and reports commit statuses back to GitHub, so developers keep working in GitHub.
Build chains with snapshot dependencies, artifact reuse, and parallel tests
Test history and flaky test detection
Pipelines in Kotlin DSL, YAML, or a visual editor
Self-hosted and cloud agents in one pool, including macOS, Windows, and GPU machines
GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure Repos, and Perforce from one server
Best for: long test suites, game studios (Unity, Unreal, Perforce), builds inside your own network, and code in more than one VCS.
In practice: one game studio we work with moved its CI/CD from self-hosted GitHub runners to TeamCity on its own servers. Stacked pull requests had pushed its shared queue to 400–500 jobs, with no way to prioritize deploys. After the switch, build times dropped by about 70%.
“The biggest challenges we had with GitHub runners were stability concerns, being deeply coupled to GitHub, and a lack of visibility into what our runners were doing at any given time. […] Instead of 10 minutes, it was three or four minutes.”
– CTO of a game studio that uses TeamCity
Learn more: TeamCity vs GitHub Actions
Jenkins and Buildkite
Jenkins is the most common companion to Actions: open source, thousands of plugins, runs anywhere. The cost moves from the invoice to your engineers’ time. Buildkite orchestrates pipelines in the cloud while builds run on your agents or Buildkite-hosted ones.
Choose this path if Actions works for most repositories, but specific workloads keep hitting its limits.
Path 3: Replace Actions, keep your code on GitHub
You can move CI entirely and keep repositories, pull requests, and code review on GitHub. Your builds no longer depend on Actions’ availability, runner limits, or pricing (though if GitHub itself is down, no CI can fetch your code). Many teams migrate one pipeline at a time.
What the migration looks like
A simple Java pipeline in GitHub Actions:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
      - run: ./gradlew build test
The same pipeline in TeamCity’s Kotlin DSL, with pull request builds and status reporting to GitHub:
// .teamcity/settings.kts
import jetbrains.buildServer.configs.kotlin.*
import jetbrains.buildServer.configs.kotlin.buildFeatures.commitStatusPublisher
import jetbrains.buildServer.configs.kotlin.buildFeatures.pullRequests
import jetbrains.buildServer.configs.kotlin.buildSteps.gradle
import jetbrains.buildServer.configs.kotlin.triggers.vcs

version = "2025.11"

project {
    buildType(Build)
}

object Build : BuildType({
    name = "Build and test"

    vcs { root(DslContext.settingsRoot) }

    steps {
        gradle {
            tasks = "build test"
            jdkHome = "%env.JDK_21_0%"
        }
    }

    triggers { vcs { } }

    features {
        pullRequests {
            provider = github {
                authType = vcsRoot()
                filterTargetBranch = "+:refs/heads/main"
            }
        }
        commitStatusPublisher {
            publisher = github {
                githubUrl = "https://api.github.com"
                authType = vcsRoot()
            }
        }
    }
})
authType = vcsRoot() requires a VCS root that uses an access token over HTTPS.
It’s longer, but it’s code: autocompletion, refactoring, and reuse instead of copy-pasted YAML. Rewriting configuration by hand is the most common migration difficulty in our survey, so move one pipeline at a time.
“Don’t be afraid of converting all of your GitHub runner YAML into Kotlin DSL. It’s actually really easy to get started, and it is way more powerful than GitHub runners because it is a full Turing-complete language.”
– CTO of a game studio that uses TeamCity
Other GitHub Actions alternatives for this path
CircleCI: test splitting, parallelism, and SSH reruns of failed jobs. Since September 2026, it can run GitHub Actions workflow files (open preview, Linux only).
GitLab CI/CD: builds GitHub repositories through CI/CD for external repositories (Premium and Ultimate).
Buildkite and Jenkins (see path 2).
Choose this path if Actions is a bottleneck across most repositories, but GitHub itself works fine for you.
Path 4: Leave GitHub altogether
This makes sense when the problem is GitHub itself: lock-in, compliance, or a company-wide platform change.
GitLab CI/CD: the all-in-one DevSecOps platform. 22% of Actions organizations in our survey also use it.
Azure DevOps: for Microsoft-centric enterprises, though Microsoft’s investment is visibly shifting to GitHub.
Bitbucket Pipelines: for Atlassian shops.
Forgejo / Gitea Actions: self-hosted forges with CI modeled on GitHub Actions; existing workflows may need tweaks.

Survey usage and how each tool fits
GitHub Actions alternatives compared

ToolPathUsed by GHA orgs*Works with GitHubPricing modelThink twice if

GitHub Actions (baseline)––NativePer minute + included usageYou need on-prem control or predictable costs at scale
Third-party runners1n/a**NativePer minuteYour problem isn’t compute
TeamCity2, 37%Yes (PR builds, commit statuses)Free up to 3 agents, then per agent (On-Premises); per committer (Cloud)You only need a few simple workflows
Jenkins2, 325%Yes, via pluginsFree; you pay in maintenanceYou don’t have dedicated CI expertise
Buildkite2, 32%YesPer active user + hosted agent minutesYou want a single all-in-one platform
CircleCI35%YesCreditsUsage is spiky and hard to forecast
GitLab CI/CD3, 422%Yes, in Premium and UltimatePer user + compute minutesYou only want CI, not a whole platform
Azure DevOps2, 414%YesPer parallel job (+ per user beyond 5)You’re not invested in Azure
AWS CodePipeline / CodeBuild211%YesPer pipeline (V1) or action minute (V2) + build minutesYou run multi-cloud or on-prem
Bitbucket Pipelines46%No (Bitbucket Cloud only)Build minutesYou’re not on Bitbucket
Forgejo / Gitea Actions4n/a**NoFree (open source)You need enterprise support





* Share of the 388 surveyed organizations that use GitHub Actions and also use this tool. ** Not a survey option. Pricing models checked on vendor pages on November 19, 2026.
When TeamCity is the wrong choice
You have a few simple workflows on one repository. Actions’ included usage is hard to beat.
Your only problem is runner speed or cost. Try path 1 first.
You’re leaving GitHub and want one platform for everything. Look at GitLab.
Do you need a GitHub Actions alternative?
Most teams shouldn’t leave. But if two or more of these apply, it’s probably time to add a second tool:
Your CI minutes bill has exploded.
You spend real time keeping self-hosted runners healthy.
Some builds need hardware or networks GitHub-hosted runners can’t provide.
Only a handful of people can change your workflow YAML.
A GitHub outage stops releases and deployments, not just CI.
Part of your code lives outside GitHub.
Whichever path you choose, if you keep any workflows on Actions, three habits make them much harder to attack:
Use OIDC instead of stored cloud keys. With OIDC, each workflow run gets a short-lived token from your cloud provider, so there are no long-lived secrets to steal.
Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA, not a version tag. A tag like @v4 can be moved to point at different code, which is how the trivy-action attack worked. A full commit SHA always points at the same code.
Give each workflow only the permissions it needs. Set permissions: in the workflow file so the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN can’t write to your repository unless a job really has to.

TeamCity
Keep GitHub. Add the missing piece.
Your code stays on GitHub. TeamCity runs the builds that Actions struggles with.

Builds your GitHub pull requests and reports statuses back to them
Takes on long test suites, on-prem environments, Mac and GPU agents, and game builds
Free on-premises for up to 3 build agents, or 14 days free in TeamCity Cloud

Get startedOr download TeamCity On-Premises →




Related reading: Best CI/CD tools · The State of CI/CD in 2026 · Top version control tools · TeamCity vs. GitHub Actions
Methodology
Survey. CI/CD Tools Adoption Survey 2026 by TeamCity and JetBrains Research, July–August 2026. 838 respondents answered the question about their organization’s CI/CD tools; 280 named GitHub Actions as primary. Results are weighted. Open-ended answers were clustered with AI assistance and reviewed manually. Small subgroups (n=43) are directional.
Public discussions. To understand the recurring complaints about Actions, we read public developer discussions on Reddit and in GitHub Community. We use them only as context: we don’t quote or identify individual users, and every number in this post comes from our survey or from GitHub’s availability reports.
Incidents. GitHub’s monthly availability reports, January–October 2026 (57 incidents). An incident counts if GitHub’s description mentions Actions, workflow runs, or runners. Durations are GitHub’s own figures.
Tool selection. Every CI/CD tool used by at least 2% of Actions organizations in the survey, plus third-party runners and Forgejo / Gitea Actions, which weren’t survey options but come up often as alternatives.
FAQ
What is the best GitHub Actions alternative? It depends on what you want to change. For faster or cheaper compute, a third-party runner is enough. To keep your code on GitHub and get complex builds, on-prem hardware, and predictable costs, look at TeamCity, Jenkins, or Buildkite. If you’re moving your code too, GitLab or Azure DevOps.
Are there free GitHub Actions alternatives? Jenkins, Forgejo / Gitea Actions, and Woodpecker are open source. GitLab, CircleCI, Buildkite, and Bitbucket Pipelines have free tiers, and TeamCity On-Premises is free for up to 3 build agents.
Why are developers moving away from GitHub Actions? Mostly cost, performance, and reliability: GitHub reported 21 incidents affecting Actions in the first ten months of 2026. Most teams, though, add a second tool rather than leave.
Is GitHub Actions or Jenkins better? Actions is easier to start with and built into GitHub. Jenkins gives you full control and runs anywhere, but you maintain it. 25% of Actions organizations also run Jenkins.
Are third-party runners cheaper than GitHub-hosted runners? Usually, per minute. But they only change where jobs run: YAML, debugging, and GitHub outages stay the same.
Can I keep my code on GitHub and use a different CI/CD tool? Yes. TeamCity, Jenkins, CircleCI, Buildkite, and Azure Pipelines all build GitHub repositories and report statuses to pull requests.
Is GitHub Actions free? Standard runners are free for public repositories. Private repositories get a monthly allowance ($12 on Free, $18 on Team, $300 on Enterprise Cloud), then pay per minute: $0.006 Linux, $0.010 Windows, $0.062 macOS. Self-hosted runners are free.
