posts.creator: Andrey Koltsov
posts.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): What It Means for TeamCity
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Summary
On November 17, 2026, CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption vulnerability in the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder of several Java runtimes, was publicly disclosed. This vulnerability allows malicious Base64 input to corrupt JVM process memory, potentially causing a crash or remote code execution.
The issue is not a vulnerability in TeamCity itself. However, TeamCity’s server and build agents run on Java versions that may contain the vulnerable code. Our security assessment has identified a potential exploitation scenario, so we strongly recommend updating to the latest version to mitigate the risk.
Recommended actions:
TeamCity On-Premises: Review every server node and build agent, and apply one of the mitigations described below. The complete fix is to update the Java runtime used by each component. You can apply an interim JVM flag if an immediate update is not possible.
TeamCity Cloud: Servers and JetBrains-hosted agents are not affected. However, you should still review the Java runtimes used by self-hosted build agents.
Details
The vulnerability is in an optimized Base64 decoder that affects Java runtimes used on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI). When an application passes attacker-controlled Base64 input to the affected decoder, the decoder can write past the end of a heap buffer and corrupt process memory. The impact depends on how the application handles that input.
Exposure is limited to systems that meet both of the following conditions:
They use Java 17, 21, 25, 27, or Oracle Java 8 Performance Pack (version 8u511-perf or earlier), without the appropriate security fix.
They use an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI.




Since TeamCity is a Java application, the exposure of its server and build agents depends on the underlying Java runtime.
What you need to do
1. Identify affected hosts
A host is affected if both of the following conditions are true. Run the relevant checks on every server node and build agent, including inside Docker containers.
The Java version is older than the fixed version listed below. Note that TeamCity might not use the same Java version as the one in PATH. You can also check the version in the server or agent startup logs.
java -version
The CPU supports the AVX-512 VBMI set extension:
Linux
# Affected if returns "avx512vbmi"
grep -Eom1 'avx512_?vbmi' /proc/cpuinfo
macOS (Intel only)
# Affected if returns "AVX512VBMI"
sysctl -n machdep.cpu.leaf7_features | grep -ow AVX512VBMI
Windows (PowerShell 7.4+)
# Affected if returns "True"
[System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.Avx512Vbmi]::IsSupported
2. Mitigate
There are two mitigation options:
Option A (recommended): Update the Java runtime.
Option B: If an immediate update is not possible, disable the vulnerable intrinsic as an interim mitigation.
After performing either option, check the result as described in the Verify section below.
Option A: Update the Java runtime
Update each affected runtime to a fixed build – one of the versions below or a newer one:

Release lineOracle / OpenJDKAmazon Corretto

1717.0.21.117.0.21.1.2
2121.0.13.121.0.13.1.2
2525.0.5.125.0.5.1.2
2727.0.1.127.0.1.1.4
8 (Oracle Performance Pack only)8u513-perfCorretto 8 is not affected





For other distributions, use the fixed build from your Java vendor.
Server: Follow the instructions on the Install non-bundled version of Java page of the TeamCity documentation. Note that <TeamCity Home>/jre takes precedence over JAVA_HOME.
Agent: Follow the instructions on the Path to Java on Agent Machine documentation page.
TeamCity Docker images: The images for TeamCity 2026.1.6 and 2026.2.2 have been republished with a patched Java runtime – the TeamCity versions themselves remain unchanged. We recommend updating to these images. If upgrading is not feasible, follow these instructions to patch your existing images.




Restart each component and recreate Docker containers.
Option B: Disable the vulnerable intrinsic
Both of the following JVM options prevent the vulnerable code from running. Use only one of them.
Disable the accelerated Base64 routines. The JVM stops using the hardware-accelerated Base64 code and uses regular compiled code instead. This affects the performance of Base64-heavy workloads:
 -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics
Limit the JVM to AVX2. In this case, the JVM won’t generate AVX-512 code at all (including Base64 decoded), which has a broader performance impact. On ARM64, it prevents startup unless -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions is also set:
 -XX:UseAVX=2
Neither option comes from Oracle or the OpenJDK project: The researchers who disclosed the issue identified them, and security vendors (Datadog and VulnCheck) have verified them.
To apply the chosen option (shown below as <option>):
Server: Append it to the TEAMCITY_SERVER_OPTS environment variable.
Agent started by agent.sh or agent.bat: Append it to both TEAMCITY_AGENT_OPTS (the agent process) and TEAMCITY_LAUNCHER_OPTS (the launcher process).
Agent running as a Windows service: In <agent home>/launcher/conf/wrapper.conf:

Add wrapper.app.parameter.<N>=<option> before the jetbrains.buildServer.agent.AgentMain line.
Add wrapper.java.additional.<N>=<option>.
Renumber the lines that follow each insertion.
Docker: Append it to the environment variables in the server (TEAMCITY_SERVER_OPTS) or agent (TEAMCITY_AGENT_OPTS) containers.




Restart each component and recreate Docker containers. A running JVM keeps the options it was started with. Remove the option once the runtime is updated.
Verify
Ensure that each TeamCity component is running on the updated JDK version or, if you’re using an interim workaround, has been started with the required JVM option.
You can verify this in the server or agent startup logs. For example:
... 
Java: 21.0.13.1, OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (21.0.13.1+2-LTS, mixed mode, sharing), OpenJDK Runtime Environment (21.0.13.1+2-LTS), Amazon.com Inc.; JVM parameters: ...-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics
... 
Frequently asked questions
Is TeamCity affected?
TeamCity may use affected Java runtimes on x86-64 hosts. We strongly recommend updating affected Java runtimes on TeamCity servers and build agents, or applying an appropriate mitigation.
Do I need to upgrade TeamCity?
The fix is applied to the Java runtime, and upgrading TeamCity does not necessarily replace it. We will provide additional mitigation mechanisms with the upcoming TeamCity 2026.2.3 and 2026.1.7.
Are ARM CPUs affected?
The vulnerable code exists only in the x86-64 JVM. ARM64 hosts, including Apple silicon and AWS Graviton, are not affected.
Is every x86-64 CPU affected?
Only processors with AVX-512 VBMI support running specific Java versions are affected. Use the detection script to check whether this applies to a specific host.
Support
For any questions regarding this issue, please get in touch with the TeamCity Support team by submitting a ticket. To report a security issue in TeamCity, please follow our Coordinated Disclosure Policy.
References
National Vulnerability Database, CVE-2026-114938
Oracle Critical Security Patch Update, November 2026
Amazon Corretto changelogs: 17, 21, 25, 27
CISA alert: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
Datadog Security Labs analysis: Java4Shell: Remote Code Execution in OpenJDK
VulnCheck analysis: Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: Fine, I Guess We’ll Do This Again

posts.title: Vulkan Rendering Is Now The Default on Linux Wayland
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
JetBrains IDEs are adopting a new rendering path on Linux. As you may remember, our IDEs started running in native Wayland mode in Linux Wayland sessions with 2026.1. Starting from 2026.3, the Vulkan rendering pipeline is enabled by default in this setup.
Nothing changes for X11, XWayland, or other operating systems. Vulkan rendering is not yet supported in Remote Development mode, but we’re planning to add this in one of the 2026.3 bugfix versions, following additional compatibility work.
Why Vulkan?
The rendering pipeline is the part of the IDE responsible for drawing the editor, tool windows, dialogs, popups, and other UI elements. Before 2026.3, native Wayland sessions used software rendering by default. Native Wayland provides a modern windowing and scaling model, but without Vulkan, the IDE’s graphics subsystem relies on software rendering. The window image is then kept in system RAM, while the CPU converts UI primitives – such as lines, rectangles, curves, text, and effects – into pixels. See this blog post for a more technical explanation. Although this work has been heavily optimized, it still consumes CPU resources that could be used for other tasks.
The cost becomes most visible when a large or complex area of the IDE has to be redrawn, for example when resizing a window, scrolling, typing, or displaying popups. Fractional display scaling makes the effect more noticeable because a non-integer scale requires the renderer to produce and compose more pixels.
This helps explain why a native Wayland session might have felt laggy, even on a system with a powerful GPU: The GPU wasn’t doing the main rendering work. Switching to the X11 toolkit could improve rendering performance by reducing the amount of work done by the CPU, but at the cost of native Wayland behavior and potentially blurrier output in the case of fractional scaling. 
Vulkan keeps the native Wayland path while moving more of the rendering work from the CPU to the GPU. The actual performance benefits depend on the GPU, driver, desktop environment, and workload, so the improvement will not be identical on all systems.
The result is a stronger foundation for a responsive, modern IDE experience on Linux Wayland, particularly on systems with fractional display scaling or complex UI content.
Vulkan is designed to produce the same visual output as the other rendering backends, but with better responsiveness and reduced power consumption. The goal here is to improve efficiency in image rendering, not change the way the image looks.
How to tell whether Vulkan is enabled
Starting with version 2026.3, Vulkan rendering is enabled by default when you run your IDE in a native Linux Wayland session. No additional configuration is required. 
If you previously switched to the X11 toolkit but are now running native Wayland sessions on Linux, make sure you remove the following option from Help | Edit custom VM options:
-Dsun.awt.toolkit.name=XToolkit
Then restart your IDE.
What comes next
We are continuing to improve the Vulkan rendering pipeline and native Wayland support with different Linux distributions, desktop environments, GPUs, drivers, and display configurations based on internal testing and user feedback.
Upcoming bug-fix releases will be focused on making the default behavior in a Wayland session more robust, especially in areas where users are more likely to notice issues. For example, our upcoming plans include:
Adding missing Java 2D primitives to fix problems affecting color emoji and some shapes, as well as to close remaining visual gaps.
Improving text rendering at fractional display scaling, where some configurations can still produce blurry fonts.
Addressing issues with window presentation and incorrectly rendered views.
Bringing Vulkan to additional usage scenarios, including remote development, once the remaining compatibility prerequisites are met.
The JetBrains Runtime roadmap also includes deeper GPU acceleration for antialiased geometry. This should allow more UI drawing operations to benefit from hardware acceleration instead of falling back to less efficient paths. 
The longer-term goal is to make the Wayland toolkit and its Vulkan pipeline suitable for broader OpenJDK use, while also exploring Vulkan-based rendering for Linux X11.
Help us improve Vulkan on Linux
Despite our efforts to stabilize Vulkan rendering in the officially supported configurations, some hardware and software combinations may still produce unexpected results.
If you encounter rendering artifacts, flickering, missing content, crashes, or unexpectedly slow performance, please report the issue through our usual support channels, such as YouTrack or the support request form.
When reporting an issue, please include the following:
The IDE name and build number.
Your Linux distribution and desktop environment.
Your GPU, graphics driver version, and display scaling factor.
A screenshot or screen recording if the problem is visual.
Complete IDE logs captured via Help | Collect logs and diagnostic data.
Steps to reproduce the issue.
This information helps us narrow down where the problem originated: in the IDE, JetBrains Runtime, the desktop environment, or the graphics driver. It also helps us prioritize improvements for future releases.
If you encounter problems with rendering and suspect they may be caused by Vulkan, go to Help | Edit custom VM options… and add the following option:
-Dsun.java2d.vulkan=false
Then restart your IDE.
We hope Vulkan rendering will make our IDEs feel more responsive and consistent for Linux Wayland users. As always, we will continue refining the implementation and delivering improvements in upcoming releases

posts.title: JetBrains Air in GoLand: Build, Review, and Profile Go Code With Agents
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
If you’ve ever built backend services in Go, chances are you’ve also written a webhook handler or two. They’re small and rarely get much attention – that is, until something breaks. A third-party provider sends a signed request, and then you check the signature, store the event, and reply. Sounds like three easy steps, but a lot can go wrong. A captured request could get replayed, a duplicate could get saved twice, or a forged signature could slip through. 
Coding agents are not likely to make these types of mistakes, so with code becoming cheaper to generate, handlers are a good task to give them. They can also write handlers faster than you can. But even with their suitability to the task, it is still on you to check that they got the details right if you want to avoid issues in production.
That’s where JetBrains Air in IDEs comes in. It gives you one place to start your preferred agents, follow their progress, and review their work. In this article, we’ll build a small webhook receiver, review the changes and send feedback straight from the diff, and then run a few follow-up tasks in parallel, each in its own worktree, that will all be merged together later. Finally, we’ll verify the combined output with GoLand’s tools, including the HTTP client and database tools. And to make things easier, we’ll let an agent profile the handler with our new profiling skill, goland-profiler.
Tag along to see how to create a working service you own and trust in a matter of minutes.
What we’re building
Our example is a small service that receives signed, Stripe-style payment webhooks and stores each event just once. We start with an empty Go module with nothing in it but a brief, BRIEF.md, that agents will use as a reference. You can copy it from the demo repository: air-goland-demo. 
These are the principles of our project:
Standard library only: Our project uses net/http for routing, log/slog for logging, and an in-memory store, so the service runs with go run and needs no extra setup.
One endpoint only: POST /webhooks/{provider} accepts a JSON event and stores it once by its ID. A new event gets 202 Accepted, and a redelivery gets 200 OK.
Signed requests: Every request carries a signature, and anything with a missing or invalid signature, or a timestamp older than five minutes, gets 401 Unauthorized.
Laying out the core principles is something you don’t necessarily want to hand off to agents straight away, because that’s where you decide on the definition of “done”. Also, because several agents will use it at the same time, the brief is what ties their work together. Naturally, the better you scope your project, the easier it will be for the agents to follow along and make fewer mistakes.
First, we’ll ask an agent to build the service from BRIEF.md – the store, the handler, the signature check, and main.go. Once that’s in place, we’ll take on three follow-up tasks: an SQLite store, extra tests for the signature check, and a set of signed test requests for GoLand’s HTTP client. When we’re done, the core of the service should resemble our demo repository – a reference version of the service you can use to try out our new Profiling skill (more on that later). The reference keeps only the in-memory store, so it doesn’t include the SQLite store or the HOOKRELAY_DB setting your agent adds.




Getting started with Air in GoLand
In GoLand 2026.3, Air has become the default AI workspace (replacing AI Assistant), so there’s nothing to install – you’ll see it on your home screen after you update. You can choose which agents you want to work with, including Junie, Codex, Claude Code, or any other agent that supports the Agent Client Protocol (ACP).
There are three ways to start a session:
Agent widget: Click the widget in the main toolbar to start a session with your current preset, or click the drop-down button next to it to pick a different agent.
Agent Sessions tool window: Open it with View | Tool Windows | Agent Sessions.
Global prompt: Press Ctrl twice anywhere in the IDE, type your request, and press Enter. If you have code selected in the editor, it will be used as context.
Each session opens in its own tab. You can pick the model, the effort, and the access level (i.e. how much oversight the agent has). The first time you send a request, the agent may ask you to authorize it – with your service account, JetBrains AI, or a provider key you add under Settings | AI | Air | Accounts.
Launch your first agent task
First, we’re going to hand off the core of the service to Codex. With a properly defined scope, one agent with a sufficiently robust model should be able to build this simple service without any major hiccups.
In the Agent Sessions tool window, click the drop-down button next to New Session and select Codex.
Pick a model in the model selector below the text field.
Enter the prompt and press Enter.
Here’s the prompt we used:
Build the service described in BRIEF.md: an in-memory event store behind a Store interface in internal/store, the webhook handler in internal/webhook, signature verification as net/http middleware in internal/middleware, and a main.go file that wires them together. Store each event once by its ID, replying 202 Accepted for a new event and 200 OK for a duplicate, and log with log/slog. Add table-driven tests and a benchmark for the handler.




Review changes
The easy part is done. Now it’s time to make sense of what the agent produced and see if it’s done everything right.
When an agent finishes a turn, the session lists the files it changed, with added and removed lines, under Since last turn. Click a file to open its diff, or click Review to step through all of them. Since this session works directly in your project, its changes also show up in the Commit tool window (⌘K). For sessions that run in a worktree, which we’ll get to shortly, Worktree Changes in the session header shows everything the agent has changed compared to the base branch.




Luckily enough, webhook receivers fail in pretty predictable ways. This is where your actual experience as a developer comes in handy. Instead of reading the diff top to bottom, you can check it against a short list of known offenders:
Constant-time comparison: Signatures should be compared with hmac.Equal. A plain == or bytes.Equal returns at the first mismatched byte, which can leak how much of a forged signature was right.
Raw body: The HMAC has to cover the timestamp and the body exactly as it arrived, not a re-encoded version of the parsed JSON.
Replay window: Stale timestamps should be rejected, or a captured request can be replayed indefinitely.
Size limit: Without http.MaxBytesReader, a client can send a body of any size, and the service will read all of it.
Read once: If the middleware reads r.Body to check the signature, it has to put it back for the handler.
Idempotent replies: Providers retry anything that doesn’t get a 2xx response, so duplicates – including one that loses a race to be saved – should get 200 OK.
Quiet errors: Error responses should carry a short, fixed message, while the details go to the logs. We covered this in our guide to secure error handling in Go.
Give feedback in the diff
If you find any mistakes, you can describe each change you want in the chat, but it’s quicker and leaves less room for error to point the agent at the right line of code instead. In the diff, click the chat icon in the gutter next to a line or selection of lines, type your note, and click Add Note or press Enter. You can also leave several notes and send them together.




Once you send the message, the notes stay attached to it as a read-only record of what you asked for. The agent picks up from there, and its next Since last turn list shows only what changed since then.
When you’re happy with the results, commit them from the Commit tool window (⌘K). This will be our starting point for subsequent tasks.
Run more tasks in parallel
Normally, you’d probably complete the tasks that we’ll work on in a sequence. But since they don’t really depend on each other, you can hand them out to agents all at the same time and review the changes as they come in. We’re going to create:
SQLite store: A persistent store behind the existing Store interface.
Tests for the replay window: Proof that the signature middleware rejects requests that are more than five minutes old.
Signed test requests: A way to try the whole service from GoLand’s HTTP client.
We will work with worktrees, so that agents don’t get in each other’s way. Here’s how to set them up:
In the Agent Sessions tool window, click the drop-down button next to New Session and select the agent.
Open the run mode list in the toolbar above the text field and select New Local Worktree. The session will get its own Git worktree and a branch.
In the branch list next to the project name, choose the branch with your first commit as the base.
Pick a model in the model selector below the text field.
Enter the prompt and press Enter.
We’re going to give the SQLite store to Claude with this prompt:
Add an SQLite implementation of the Store interface in internal/store, using the pure-Go driver modernc.org/sqlite, so the service still runs with go run. Make the event ID the primary key, so a duplicate insert returns the same error as the in-memory store. In main.go, use SQLite when HOOKRELAY_DB is set to a file path, and keep the in-memory store as the default. Add table-driven tests against a temporary database. The driver is the one exception to the brief’s standard-library rule.
The other two tasks are pretty routine, so they’re a good fit for Junie Lite – our coding agent with a cost-efficient model for everyday tasks that works with your JetBrains Account. Here are the prompts:
Add table-driven tests for the signature middleware in internal/middleware to check that a request is rejected with 401 Unauthorized when its timestamp is more than five minutes old, and accepted when it’s just inside the window. Only change test files.
Create requests/webhooks.http for GoLand’s HTTP client with three requests to POST {{host}}/webhooks/stripe: a valid event, the same event sent again, and an event with a bad signature. Sign the first two in a pre-request script, as described in BRIEF.md. In a dev environment, put the host in requests/http-client.env.json and the secret in requests/http-client.private.env.json. Give each request a response check for the status code the brief expects.
All three agents now work side by side, each in its own worktree. The Agent Sessions tool window shows which sessions are In Progress, which need your input, and which have finished with results you haven’t looked at yet, so there’s no need to keep clicking through tabs to check. If you turn on Time and Cost under the Filter icon, you can also see how long each session has been running and what it has cost so far.




If an agent needs a decision from you – like permission to run go test – its session is marked as waiting for input, and you can answer right in its tab. You can also queue follow-up prompts while an agent is busy. They’re sent as soon as it finishes its current turn.
Tie it all together
Each of the new additions has only been tested on its own – the SQLite store against a temporary file and the new tests against the middleware, while the test requests haven’t been sent anywhere yet. So now that we want to combine the branches, it’s time to check the whole thing.
First, you want to review each worktree the same way you did the original service: Review the changes and leave notes in the diff.
Be mindful that test requests have to sign exactly what the middleware checks, ensuring that the same string with the same secret in the same header format. The secret belongs in the http-client.private.env.json, not in the shared environment file or the script.
Once you’re happy with the results, you can bring these three branches together:
In your project, check out the branch the work should land on. Air cherry-picks onto whichever branch is currently checked out, not the worktree’s base branch.
In each session’s header, click the drop-down button next to Commit, select Commit, and cherry-pick all.




Send the test requests
The private environment file is in .gitignore, so Junie Lite’s copy stayed behind in its worktree. Create your own in requests/http-client.private.env.json:
{"dev": {"secret": "dev-secret"}}
Next, start the service with SQLite: Open the run configuration for main.go (Run | Edit), add HOOKRELAY_DB=hookrelay.db under Environment, and run it. Then open requests/webhooks.http, select dev in the Run with list, and click Run All Requests in File.




A pre-request script signs each request before it’s sent, and a response check after each one compares the status code with what the brief expects. That means you don’t have to read the responses yourself – the Tests tab of the Services tool window lists each check as passed or failed.
Check the database
The database tells you what the HTTP client stored. Open the Database tool window, click +, choose Data Source | SQLite, and point it at hookrelay.db in the project folder. GoLand may offer to download the SQLite driver first. Next, open the events table, or run a quick query in the query console (adjust the table and column names to whatever your agent chose):
SELECT id, COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY id;
The valid event and its duplicate should leave one row between them. Since the database keeps its data between runs, delete hookrelay.db before you send the requests again, or the valid event becomes a duplicate and its check fails.




Let an agent profile the handler
Voilà! Our agents’ service works, but for now, nothing tells us how it behaves under load. Webhooks tend to arrive in bursts – after an outage, for example, when a provider redelivers its whole backlog at once – so a slow handler is more than a theoretical problem. Normally, this is where you’d reach for the profiler. With GoLand 2026.3, you can hand that job to an agent, too.
To demonstrate the profiling skill on an actual problem, we’ll switch to a reference version of this service that you can find on GitHub. It’s a finished receiver built to the same brief, with one difference: We’ve left a performance problem in it on purpose, so you can repeat every step below on your own machine.
Where skills can help
A skill is a set of instructions that teaches an agent how to handle a specific type of task. On its own, an agent can only work with what it sees from the outside: It reads the code, runs commands, and parses their output. GoLand’s skills connect supported agents to the IDE’s own tools so that the agents can use them more effectively, allowing the agents to know which profile to take, how to read it, and how to tell whether a fix actually worked.
The goland-profiler skill is bundled with Air and works with Claude Code, Codex, and Junie. These agents can run your application with GoLand’s profiler, record a CPU profile while it handles traffic, and read its hot paths and line-level hints. Thanks to the skill, there’s nothing to set up – the agent loads the skill when a task calls for it, or you can attach it explicitly by typing / in the prompt or by clicking Add and choosing Skills.




How to use it
To try out the skill, open the demo repo in GoLand and stay on its main branch. The service needs traffic to profile, so the repo comes with a small load generator that sends signed events for 30 seconds. Start a new session with this prompt:
Run the service with /goland-profiler and record a CPU profile while go run ./cmd/loadgen sends it traffic. Tell me where the handler spends its CPU time and memory, and what you would change. Don’t edit any code yet.
We suggest asking for a diagnosis first so that you can check the agent’s reading of the profile before it acts, and decide what you want to change based on evidence.
The agent starts the service with the profiler, records CPU while the load generator runs, reads the hot paths, and comes back with the culprit: validateEventID compiles its regular expression on every call. In our run, validateEventID accounted for 69% of the CPU use, with regexp.MustCompile being the hottest call. The allocation churn was keeping the garbage collector busy on top of that.




You don’t have to take the agent’s word for it, though. The profile it captured is an ordinary Go profile, so you can open it in the Go Optimization tool window and look at the flame graph yourself, where regexp.MustCompile sits right under validateEventID and takes up most of the handler’s width.
The fix is pretty straightforward: Compile the pattern once, at the package level, instead of compiling on every request.
// Before: the pattern is compiled on every call
func validateEventID(id string) error {
	var eventIDPattern = regexp.MustCompile("^evt_[A-Za-z0-9]{24}$")

	if !eventIDPattern.MatchString(id) {
		return fmt.Errorf("invalid event id %q", id)
	}

	return nil
}
// After: the pattern is compiled once, when the package is initialized
var eventIDPattern = regexp.MustCompile("^evt_[A-Za-z0-9]{24}$")

func validateEventID(id string) error {
	if !eventIDPattern.MatchString(id) {
		return fmt.Errorf("invalid event id %q", id)
	}

	return nil
}
Sharing one compiled pattern across all requests is safe in this case, since a *regexp.Regexp can be used by multiple goroutines at the same time, but it’s worth confirming first before you let your agent run loose. We asked the agent to apply the fix and profile the service again under the same load. To put numbers on the difference, we also ran BenchmarkHandler before and after.

BeforeAfter
Time per request13,141 ns2,748 ns
Bytes per request16.4 KB6.7 KB
Allocations per request12625





After the change, the benchmark is about 4.6 times faster with 59% fewer bytes and 80% fewer allocations per request. Times will vary by machine, but the drop in bytes and allocations should be about the same.
Try it yourself
You can repeat this exercise on your own machine to play with the skill. The repository has two branches:
main: a finished service with a planted slow event ID validation.
fixed (use for reference): the same service with the regular expression compiled once.
To try it out:
Clone the repository and open it in GoLand 2026.3. You’ll need Go 1.27.3 or later.
Start an Air session with Claude Code, Codex, or Junie.
Ask the agent to profile the running service – you can use the prompt from the previous section.
Once the agent has applied its fix, compare your working copy with ours by running git diff origin/fixed, or view our fix on its own with git diff origin/main origin/fixed.
Your agent’s fix doesn’t have to match ours line for line. But it should hold up against the same checks: The tests pass, and the new profile no longer has regular expression compilation at the top.
Run the final checks before you merge
Whether you’re merging the service or the profiling fix, run the checks one last time on the final code. Then, reset the store and run webhooks.http again so the first request is a new event, and restart the service if it uses the in-memory store  or delete hookrelay.db if it uses SQLite. If everything checks out, commit from the Commit tool window (⌘K) and merge the branch. A pull request is always a good place for a human to look at the changes – especially ones where three agents were in the driver’s seat.
Code the way you want
AI has changed the coding game to the point that it’s no longer a question of whether you use agents, but how you use them. At JetBrains we support all your workflows. Whether it’s in the IDE or the terminal, whether you use agents for small tasks or orchestrating entire services, whether you YOLO your way through or meticulously check every change, Air is there to help you with the one thing that hasn’t changed: your ownership of your code.
This quick demo only scratches the surface of what Air in IDEs can do, but it’s a good starting point to explore more. Let us know how you like this new addition to your IDE and what features we should demo next. And keep an eye out for more tutorials and skills in the coming months.
Happy coding,
The GoLand team

posts.title: Security Update for YouTrack Server: Java Vulnerability CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell)
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
On November 17, 2026, a critical vulnerability in Java was publicly disclosed: CVE-2026-114938, also known as Java4Shell. It affects Java runtimes used by many applications, including YouTrack Server. We have released YouTrack Server updates that include a fixed Java runtime. YouTrack Cloud is not affected.
YouTrack Cloud customers do not need to take any action.
YouTrack Server administrators should update to one of the fixed builds listed below. If you cannot update immediately, apply the temporary workaround.
Action required from YouTrack Server administrators
If you use YouTrack Server 2025.3 or later, update to the applicable fixed build:
2026.2: 2026.2.19884
2026.1: 2026.1.14193
2025.3: 2025.3.178461
You can check your current version in Administration | Server Settings | Global Settings. To see which versions are available under your license, check the License Details section in the settings or visit your JetBrains Account. To upgrade, download the latest available version from the YouTrack download page, or pick a specific build from the previous versions page. For upgrade instructions, refer to the Installation and Upgrade documentation.
If you’re running an older version or cannot update immediately, apply this temporary workaround:
Stop YouTrack.
Run this command:
youtrack configure -J-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics 
For Docker installations and other distribution types, see Configure JVM options.
Start YouTrack.
This workaround disables the part of Java that contains the vulnerability. It may make some operations slightly slower. The workaround is a temporary measure, and we recommend upgrading to a fixed build as soon as possible.
The vulnerability: Summary
The vulnerability is in Java itself, not in YouTrack’s code. It can only be triggered on servers with certain modern processors. An attacker could send a specially crafted request to crash the server or, in the worst case, run code on it.
YouTrack Cloud: Not affected. Cloud instances run on hardware where the vulnerability cannot be triggered. You do not need to take any action.
YouTrack Server: All versions that include the affected Java runtime are potentially affected. Whether a specific installation is at risk depends on the server hardware, so we recommend that all customers update.
We are not aware of any cases where this vulnerability has been exploited against YouTrack.
Mitigation
We’ve released bug-fix updates for YouTrack Server that include a fixed Java runtime. The fixed builds are listed above.
Support
If you have any questions about this issue, please get in touch with the YouTrack Support team.
Your YouTrack team

posts.title: JetBrains Plugin Developer Conf 2026: Watch All the Talks
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
JetBrains Plugin Developer Conf 2026 took place on November 10, bringing together JetBrains experts and plugin developers for a day of technical talks, practical examples, and discussions about the latest in plugin development.
This year’s program explored how AI and agents are influencing plugin development, alongside new IntelliJ Platform APIs, language support, plugin architecture, and development across different environments.
Missed the conference or want to revisit a session? All talk recordings are now available on YouTube!






What Did We Cover?
From AI-assisted development to integrating web applications and supporting WSL and Dev Containers, the sessions offer practical insights for developers building and maintaining plugins for JetBrains IDEs.
Here’s the full lineup:
Opening Keynote – Ivan Chirkov, Yuriy Artamonov, Jakub Chrzanowski, and Róbert Novotný share the latest JetBrains Marketplace and IntelliJ Platform updates, including new APIs and improvements to plugin development tools. 
Watch →
Dependency Assistant: An IntelliJ Plugin That Started With a Prompt – discusses where AI-assisted development proved useful and where it added unnecessary work.
Watch →
Building Language Plugins With the Native LSP API – Vladimir Logachev demonstrates how to build language support for JetBrains IDEs using the native LSP API. 
Watch →
Integrating a Web-Based Profiler Into IntelliJ IDEA – Johannes Bechberger explains how he integrated the Firefox Profiler into an IntelliJ plugin. 
Watch →
Your Plugin’s Second Service: Architecture for Integrations That Grow – Evgeny Kudelevsky shares lessons on designing scalable plugin architectures and exposing plugin functionality to AI agents through MCP. 
Watch →
EelApi: Developing Plugins for Every Project Environment – Alexander Koshevoy explores how EelApi simplifies plugin development across different project environments.
Watch →
Whether you’re interested in new IntelliJ Platform capabilities, building AI-powered integrations, or improving your existing plugins, you can watch the sessions at your own pace.
Thanks for Being Part of Plugin Developer Conf 2026!
Thank you to everyone who joined us live, asked questions, and contributed to the discussions, and to our speakers and hosts for sharing their knowledge and experience.
If you’d like to stay up to date with upcoming events, IntelliJ Platform tools, and plugin development tips, subscribe to JetBrains Marketplace updates.

posts.content:encodedSnippet:
According to the JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Report 2026, GitHub is the most popular place to host code. It is used by 85.1% of developers for personal projects and by 56.0% for professional projects.
GitLab ranks second in both groups, but the gap is much smaller among those hosting professional projects there.




That difference is a useful starting point for choosing a platform. A service you use for a side project may also work well for your team. At work, though, the decision involves more people and more requirements: code reviews, access policies, existing tools, and the way you build and release software.
Below, we look at what the survey tells us about those choices, compare the main platforms, and explain where smaller services fit. We also take a separate look at game development, where a repository can contain as much artwork and audio as source code.

Share of developers, weighted survey results

90.7%regularly use Git. SVN is a distant second at 5.9%.

Source: JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026. Base: developers asked about team tools, n = 4,519.

Version control and repository hosting
Version control keeps a history of your code, so you can see what changed and go back to an earlier version. A hosting platform such as GitHub or GitLab gives your team a shared place for that code, together with reviews, permissions, and other collaboration tools.
Most platforms covered in this article work with Git, and the survey shows why: 90.7% of developers use Git, while Subversion is down to 5.9%. Perforce and Unity Version Control offer different systems for managing code and project files.

For a public project, GitHub’s familiarity can be an advantage. Contributors may already have accounts and know the pull request workflow. A team choosing a shared development platform has more to consider, including where the service can run and how code review connects to builds and releases.
GitLab deserves a closer look in that comparison than the personal-project figures alone would suggest.
The rest of the development setup matters
GitLab’s professional usage is more than double its personal-project usage. For Azure DevOps, it’s three times as high. Bitbucket also has stronger workplace adoption.
The appeal goes beyond code hosting. GitLab brings repositories and CI/CD together, Bitbucket connects with Jira, and Azure Repos works alongside Azure Boards and Azure Pipelines. 
For teams already using these tools, those connections can matter more than where individual developers keep their side projects.
Further reading: Bamboo End of Life: How to Prepare and Choose the Right CI/CD Replacement
Bitbucket is losing ground, while GitHub grows for personal projects
Comparing 2025 and 2026 using the same question wording shows one clear shift. Bitbucket’s workplace share fell from 13.7% to 9.1%, and its personal-project share halved from 6.2% to 3.0%. Both drops are statistically significant. 
Over the same period, GitHub’s share for personal projects grew from 83.2% to 86.3%, while GitLab’s numbers stayed within the margin of error.

Lower adoption doesn’t mean less useful
A tool’s overall adoption doesn’t necessarily reflect how well that tool suits a particular team’s needs. For example, in the responses to questions about general hosting, Perforce accounts for just 1.0% of professional use. In the separate game development question, it appears at 4.3%, while Unity Version Control is at 6.7%.
These adoption numbers may seem low, but ultimately teams choose these tools because of the specific files and workflows they support. ‘Popularity’ doesn’t tell the whole story, because a less popular tool may still excel within its own niche use cases. It all just depends on how your team actually works with assets.

The same applies to Gitea, Forgejo, and Codeberg. Their smaller numbers give them less visibility in an overall ranking, but they offer different ways to host Git projects, including running your own service or using a nonprofit provider. Those are meaningful choices for developers who care about how their hosting is operated.
How to choose a hosting platform for your team
When trying out an unfamiliar platform, start by making a normal change to one of your projects. For example, a developer pushes code, opens a review, waits for the build, and merges the change. Someone else may need to approve it, or a policy may require a particular test to pass.
Ideally, you’d see how well a platform supports that entire process before making a decision about its suitability.

Evaluation checklist
What to compare during a trial

What to compareWhat it means in practice

Code reviewsCan you find reviewers, discuss changes, and require the right approvals before a merge?
Hosting and accessCan the service run where you need it, and can you manage access through your existing accounts and policies?
Repository and asset sizeHow long do developers and build agents wait for files, and what happens as storage grows?
IntegrationsDo issues, pull requests, builds, and results stay connected across your tools?
Total costWhat will you pay for the service, storage, downloads, and the time spent running it?





Try these tasks with a real repository. A small demo project won’t tell you much about cloning years of history, fetching large assets, or starting several builds at once. It is also worth checking the exact plan you would use: Review rules and administration features can differ between free and paid editions.
Also check how the platform fits the tools your developers already use day to day. In the survey, developers were just as likely to run version control operations from their IDE as from the terminal (66.5% each), and 38.3% used the hosting platform’s web interface.

Cloud hosting or running the service yourself
Choosing a platform also means deciding who runs it. GitHub, GitLab, and Gitea offer cloud-based and self-hosted options. You can also run Forgejo yourself or use Codeberg’s hosted service.
Cloud hosting means less maintenance for your team. Self-hosting gives you more control over access and storage, but your team handles updates, backups, and recovery. Factor in that time and cost, even if the software is free.
Self-hosting is a popular choice at work. About one in three developers (34.9%) report self-hosted repositories in their company, and 18.1% describe a hybrid setup. For personal projects, the cloud is the clear default at 68.6%.

Version control hosting platforms compared
The main platforms cover many of the same basics. Their differences become clearer when you look at who will use them, which tools they connect to, and how much of the setup your team wants to manage.
GitHub
Hosting: Cloud, with GitHub Enterprise Server for self-hosted installations.
GitHub is a natural starting point for a Git hosting shortlist. It brings code, pull requests, issues, and automation into a familiar interface. For projects that accept outside contributions, using a platform contributors already know can make participation easier. Organizations can also choose Enterprise Server when they need to run their own instance.
Best for: Teams that want a familiar Git workflow and a wide choice of integrations.
Strengths: Pull request collaboration, repository rules, required checks, and apps and APIs for connecting other tools.
Keep in mind: Check which controls are included in your plan, especially for private repositories. Include large-file storage and downloads in the cost estimate.
GitLab
Hosting: GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated.
GitLab is worth considering when a team wants repository hosting and delivery tools in the same place. A merge request can bring the discussion and pipeline results together, while the deployment options let the team choose who operates the service.
Best for: Teams evaluating repositories, code review, and CI/CD together.
Strengths: Merge requests, integrated pipelines, and a choice of cloud-based or self-hosted deployment.
Keep in mind: Some review controls, including required approval rules, depend on the subscription tier. A self-managed installation also needs ongoing administration.
Bitbucket
Hosting: Bitbucket Cloud and Data Center options for existing self-managed customers.
Bitbucket is most appealing to teams who already use Jira. Its integration links work items with branches, commits, and pull requests, so users can track a task without manually collecting links from several tools. The benefit is twofold: the team gets a place to host their repositories and a tighter connection between code development and their existing workflows.
Best for: Teams that already organize development work in Jira.
Strengths: Pull request reviews and links between planned work, code changes, and build or deployment information.
Keep in mind: Cloud and Data Center are different offerings. Check the available deployment and licensing path before planning a new installation or migration.
Azure DevOps and Azure Repos
Hosting: Azure DevOps Services in the cloud and Azure DevOps Server on your own infrastructure.
Azure Repos is a straightforward option to consider if your team already uses Azure DevOps. Git repositories work with pull requests and branch policies, including reviewer and build requirements. It also supports Team Foundation Version Control, or TFVC, for teams maintaining that setup.
Best for: Organizations already using Azure DevOps for work tracking and builds.
Strengths: Branch policies, pull requests, and connections with the wider Azure DevOps toolset.
Keep in mind: Decide whether the project needs Git or TFVC and whether the service will run in the cloud or on your infrastructure. Those choices affect the tools and administration involved.
Perforce P4 (formerly Helix Core)
Hosting: Self-hosted installations and P4 Cloud.
Perforce P4 deserves a place on the shortlist when large shared assets are a central part of the project. It supports file locking, streams, and workspaces that control which project files each person needs. For a game team, these can be more relevant than having the same review interface as a typical web project.
Best for: Teams working with large binary files and shared game or design assets.
Strengths: Exclusive file locking, configurable workspaces, and integrations with game development tools.
Keep in mind: Moving from Git changes how people work with version control. Include artists, developers, and build engineers in the trial so that you test the whole workflow.
Gitea
Hosting: Open-source self-hosted software, with managed and enterprise offerings.
Gitea combines Git hosting with pull requests, issues, packages, and automation. It is an option for teams who want to run their own Git service while keeping a familiar way to review and discuss changes. Gitea Actions adds CI/CD through separate runners, and external build integrations can be part of the setup too.
Best for: Teams that want to run their own Git hosting service.
Strengths: Repository collaboration, package hosting, and automation in the same installation.
Keep in mind: Someone still needs to maintain the service. If you plan to reuse GitHub Actions workflows, test them: Gitea describes its implementation as mostly compatible.
Forgejo
Hosting: Self-hosted software, also available through public hosting providers.
Forgejo offers a community-developed alternative for hosting Git projects. It grew out of Gitea and has followed its own development path since 2024. A team can run it directly or use a provider that operates it. That choice matters: the same software can come with different support, storage, and service policies depending on who runs it.
Best for: Developers who want a community-governed Git forge.
Strengths: Pull requests, issues, and Forgejo Actions, with control over a self-hosted installation.
Keep in mind: Choose the hosting provider as carefully as the software. Existing automation may need changes when moving from GitHub Actions or Gitea.
Codeberg
Hosting: Nonprofit hosted service powered by Forgejo.
Codeberg is a useful option for free and open-source projects that want a community-operated service without running a server themselves. It uses Forgejo, but choosing Codeberg is a hosting decision as well as a software decision. The service is built around supporting free software, rather than selling general-purpose private repository hosting.
Best for: Free and open-source projects looking for a nonprofit hosting provider.
Strengths: Hosted Git collaboration through Forgejo, without the work of maintaining your own instance.
Keep in mind: Read the project and resource policies. Codeberg is not intended for private commercial projects, and larger storage or CI needs may require a request.
Five more platforms worth considering
AWS CodeCommit
AWS CodeCommit is most useful for teams who want repository access to fit their AWS accounts, network setup, and audit tooling. AWS reopened the platform to new customers in November 2025. It is worth a look for that integration, while the review process and day-to-day developer experience still need to suit your team.
SourceForge
SourceForge combines Git, Mercurial, and Subversion hosting with issue tracking and software downloads. This makes it relevant to public projects that need to distribute releases as well as share source code. For those projects, the download experience is part of the product choice too.
Gitee
Gitee serves the Chinese developer ecosystem with Git hosting, code review, project collaboration, and CI/CD. It belongs in the comparison when those communities or workflows are important to the project. Check the tools and access your contributors will need, including people working from other locations.
Gogs
Gogs focuses on simple Git hosting with low resource requirements. It can run as a standalone program or in a container. It is worth considering if your team can get by with a lightweight self-hosted service. Compare its review and authentication options with your actual requirements.
SourceHut
SourceHut takes a different approach to collaboration, with Git and Mercurial hosting, mailing lists, CI, and email-based patch reviews. It’s suitable for projects that already have this workflow. If your team is used to web-based pull requests, start by trying the review process.
Why game development needs its own approach
Games include much more than code. A project can contain textures, models, animation, audio, and large scene files. Developers and artists need to share those files without overwriting each other’s work, and the build machines need to fetch them in time to produce the next playable version.
That changes what matters in version control. Changes to a source file can often be merged. Changes to a binary asset may be much harder to combine, so developers need a way to see who is working on it and prevent conflicting edits. Decisions about VCS tools also have to factor in file locking and the tools the artists are using.

Git hosting still plays a major role
GitHub is the leading platform among game developers, too, at 68.2%, followed by GitLab at 23.0%. Another 20.4% run their own Git servers. Git hosting clearly has a substantial place in game development. The decision is which combination of hosting, large-file support, and asset tools will work for a particular project.
For a Git-based setup, test Git LFS with the project’s real assets. LFS stores the file contents separately from the references kept in Git, so storage and downloads both matter. Also check locking and engine integration, rather than assuming large-file support covers the entire workflow.
Asset tools change the shortlist
Unity Version Control appears at 6.7%, alongside Bitbucket at 6.2% and Subversion at 5.5%. Perforce reaches 4.3%, and Gitea is used by 3.8%. The choices extend well beyond the platforms at the top of the general company list. Bitbucket’s decline shows up here as well: among game developers, it fell from 10.2% in 2025.
Unity Version Control provides tools for code and content creators, including file checkout and locking. Perforce offers exclusive locking and configurable workspaces. These are practical reasons to include them in an evaluation if your team spends much of its time working with large assets.
What is happening among smaller Git platforms
In free-text answers, Gitea received more workplace mentions than Forgejo: 16 vs. 3. For personal projects, the order flipped: Codeberg had 40 mentions, Forgejo 29, and Gitea 21.

The ~ symbol marks a rough estimate from free-text answers. Details of the calculation and survey bases are in the source note below.




What’s next: version control for code written with AI agents
The survey shows where teams keep their code today. A newer question is what version control should record when AI agents write part of that code. A commit shows what changed, but not the prompt, the agent’s reasoning, or the alternatives it rejected.
Entire, a company founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, is one of the most visible attempts to close that gap. Its first product, Checkpoints, is an open-source CLI that saves an agent’s session context alongside each Git commit, on a separate branch so the main history stays clean. 
Agents reinvented how we produce code. It changed our tools and half of our workflow. It’s time for the other half to catch up.
Today, we’re shipping Entire: the Git forge for agent-human collaboration. We’ve built @GoEntire using Entire. Now we want to see what you’ll build with it.

Here’s why and what’s different. 🧵
— Thomas Dohmke (@ashtom) October 26, 2026




It works with coding agents such as Claude Code and Gemini CLI. Entire launched in February 2026, so it doesn’t appear in our survey data, but it is a sign of where Git workflows may go next: Git stays the foundation, with new layers built on top for teams that work alongside agents.
Choose hosting and CI/CD platforms that match your workflow
You can choose your code hosting platform and CI/CD platform separately. For example, keep your code on GitHub and use TeamCity to build and test it.
TeamCity supports Git, Perforce, and Subversion. Its Pull Requests feature works with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps, while Commit Status Publisher sends build statuses back to your repository. Developers can see whether their checks passed without leaving the code review.
So, which platform should you choose?
GitHub is a good starting point for projects with outside contributors. GitLab brings code hosting and CI/CD together. If your team already uses Jira or Azure DevOps, Bitbucket or Azure Repos may be a natural fit.
For self-hosted Git, consider Gitea or Forgejo. Codeberg offers hosting for free software projects. Game teams working with large assets should also look at Perforce and Unity Version Control.
Use the popularity figures to narrow your options. Then try them on a real project to see how they handle your code, reviews, and builds, and how much maintenance they require.
Where the data comes from
Figures come from the JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Report 2026. Professional-use figures are based on 4,519 respondents; personal-use figures are based on the 3,280 respondents who work on personal projects. 
AWS CodeCommit, Space, and SourceForge figures and the year-over-year comparison come from a second 2026 hosting question that kept the 2025 answer list. Multiple answers were allowed; game development used a separate question with different options (n = 1,473).
The main hosting figures are weighted survey results. Values marked with a ~ symbol are rough estimates: unweighted shares of respondents who named the platform in a write-in answer. They are not official adoption rates. The fact that a solution has zero mentions does not mean it has zero use.

posts.title: Under the Hood of Native WSL Mode in RubyMine: IJent and EelApi
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
RubyMine’s WSL support has evolved over many years, resulting in several ways of working with projects in WSL. Starting with the 2026.3 release, there is one recommended way to work with a project stored in WSL – Native WSL mode: open or clone the project directly from the Welcome screen and use native WSL interpreters to run Ruby.
The IDE remains a Windows application, while a lightweight agent inside WSL handles files and processes.
Native mode and the IJent agent
To give your IDE seamless access to the Linux filesystem, processes, and other environment resources, we built IJent, a lightweight agent made just for this job. Because IJent is designed specifically for IDE workflows, we can shape its behavior, protocol, and capabilities around what developers actually need, so working with Linux feels as smooth and responsive as working locally.
Together, the IDE and IJent form a client-server pair. This may resemble the remote development model, but the server component is much thinner and more versatile.
This particular technology stack helps us address several important challenges:
Rust implementation: Rust keeps the executable slim. By not relying on Java or Kotlin for the agent, we eliminate additional runtime dependencies inside containers or WSL environments.




Transport layer: stdio provides a portable, firewall-friendly transport across all environments. Hyper-V sockets on WSL offer a faster path, which is especially beneficial for large or numerous filesystem transfers.




Correct filesystem semantics: IJent executes filesystem operations on behalf of the IDE inside the target environment. As a result, path resolution, including symbolic links, follows correct Linux semantics. Third-party plugins also benefit from this model, since their file operations are routed through IJent.
EelApi: One interface for any environment
To make full use of IJent in RubyMine, changes on the IDE side are also required. That’s where EelApi comes in.
EelApi is an API designed to abstract away the distinction between local and remote environments for everyone writing IDE-related code, including plugin authors and platform contributors.
With EelApi, developers don’t need to handle environment-specific differences themselves. The same IDE code can work across local environments, WSL, Docker, and Dev Containers without needing to know where it’s running.
In general, IJent implements the EelApi interface, providing the functionality that EelApi exposes to the IDE and plugins.
If you’re interested in a more detailed explanation of EelApi, together with a practical introduction, readThe Dev Containers Story: Introducing EelApi for Plugin Authors.
Performance tests
We conducted performance tests to compare working with remote interpreters (based on the 9P filesystem protocol) and Native mode. The results show a clear performance improvement with the new approach:




The test results represent the median of five measured runs performed on Windows 11 using WSL 2 and Ubuntu 24.04.
While Native mode is now our recommended way to work with WSL projects, the other two methods (remote development and remote interpreters) remain supported.
However, from now on we’ll be focusing our development efforts on Native WSL mode. This means other ways to work with WSL projects will no longer receive major feature updates or usability improvements, and only critical regressions will be addressed.
Thank you for reading and for all the feedback that helped us reach this point. Let us know how Native mode performs with your projects.
Follow RubyMine on X for more updates and insights.
The RubyMine team

posts.creator: Anastasia Khramushina
posts.title: LinkedIn Connected Apps 1.2: Clearer Level System, Visible Progress, and Direct Answers About Privacy
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
What if your LinkedIn profile reflected how you actually build software instead of just being a list of your skills? That’s what the LinkedIn Connected Apps plugin does: It tracks how you use your JetBrains IDE, awards you a level ranking, and provides a descriptive statement associated with your level that you can choose to share.
Since the first version came out, you’ve told us what works and what doesn’t. The level system wasn’t entirely clear and you wanted a plain explanation of what happens to your data.
Version 1.2 is built around that feedback. It introduces four levels based on real work that gets done in the IDE, a widget that shows your progress and what’s next, and a clear account of what stays on your machine.
Get the plugin
                                                    
What’s new in 1.2
Levels based on how you use your IDE
The leveling path now has four levels instead of five, and each one reflects what developers do in their IDE on a day-to-day basis. There are two distinct branches, Coding and AI, with the AI branch starting at Level 3. Because everyone starts at Level 1, you must progress through the first two levels on the Coding branch before starting on the AI branch. The branches are independent, so your Coding level and AI level can be different.
Imagine this progression, for example. Shortly after getting started with your IDE, you use code completion and reach Level 1. You continue using core functionality more broadly, searching for code throughout the project, so the next day you reach Level 2. You then start refactoring and using Git, so you reach Level 3 in Coding. Later you start working on tasks via AI chat, bringing you to Level 3 in AI. Eventually you start running AI agents and reviewing their changes, so you reach Level 4 in AI, even while you’re still at Level 3 on the Coding side. Your profile shows the level you’ve reached on each branch.

LevelCodingAI

1Use a core IDE capability, for example, search, code completion, or code navigation.–
2Search for code across the project, type with code completion, or navigate to declarations or usages.–
3Refactor by renaming or moving elements, run commands in the terminal, run your application or configurations, or use Git through the UI (commit, fetch, or update).Work on coding tasks with AI to generate and explain code, run AI agents (such as Junie, Claude, or Codex) in the integrated terminal, or complete tasks using JetBrains Air.

4Debug with the integrated debugger (Step Over, Step Into, Evaluate Expression), work with editor shortcuts, apply advanced refactorings (Extract and Introduce), and use the Git Log and Diff view.Use AI agents to generate, refactor, and explain code. Orchestrate agents or run tasks through the integrated terminal or JetBrains Air, then review their changes in the Diff view.





For more information about how levels are calculated in a particular IDE, check out the help center for IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, Rider, GoLand, CLion, RustRover, or RubyMine.
Always know what’s next
A widget shows your current level and the statement that goes with it, and explains what you’ll need to do to reach the next one. Each requirement has a progress counter and is marked with a check once completed, allowing you to track your progress at a glance and always have a clear view of what remains to be done.








For the bigger picture, switch to the tree view. It shows every level at once, including where the Coding and AI branches split at Level 3. It also marks which levels you’ve completed, which one you’re on, and which ones are still ahead. Click on any level to see exactly what it requires.




Privacy and your data
In response to your questions, here are some important details about how the plugin uses your data:
When you do something that counts toward a level, the plugin records it locally. This usage data stays on your computer and is not shared with LinkedIn. The plugin doesn’t change your IDE data sharing settings.
After you connect your LinkedIn account and reach a new level, the IDE sends only the corresponding statement.
You connect through LinkedIn’s own OAuth 2.0 page in your browser. The plugin never sees or stores your LinkedIn password. It receives only an access token and a refresh token, which it keeps in the IDE’s secure credential store.
That token lets the plugin do one thing: add and update your JetBrains IDE statement in the Connected Apps section of your profile. The plugin doesn’t read any other part of your profile.
You can end the connection at any time. Simply click Disconnect from LinkedIn in the plugin, and revoke the app’s access from your LinkedIn settings under Data privacy | Permitted services.
If you already have a statement on your profile
The statements you’ve already achieved stay as they are. Once you earn a new statement, the statement on your LinkedIn profile will also be updated.
How your existing progress carries over
If you were already using the first version of the plugin, your existing progress should generally carry over to the new four-level scheme. Here’s how the levels have changed:
Level 1 and Level 2 are unchanged.
The old Level 3 is now split into Level 3 Coding and Level 3 AI.
The old Level 4 is now split into Level 4 Coding and Level 4 AI.
The old Level 5 has been removed, and the activities associated with it have been merged into Level 4 of Coding and AI.
Your previously achieved levels will be mapped to the corresponding levels in the new scheme based on your recorded activity. In some cases, particularly when switching devices or IDEs, certain progress may not carry over completely.
How to get started
In your IDE, go to Settings | Plugins.
On the Marketplace tab, search for “LinkedIn Connected Apps” and click Install, or Update if you already have it.
Click the Your IDE Proficiency widget in the lower right corner to see your level and next steps.
When you’re ready to share your statement, click Connect to LinkedIn and follow the instructions in your browser.





The plugin is free and supports IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, Rider, GoLand, CLion, RustRover, and RubyMine, version 2025.3 or later. DataGrip isn’t supported. For the full list of level requirements, see the documentation.
Open the widget, see where you are, and let us know what you think in the comments.
FAQ
Is this a certification?
This plugin reflects how you use your IDE and doesn’t measure your skills as a developer. It is not a certification.
Do I have to share my level on LinkedIn?
Connecting to LinkedIn is totally optional. Until you connect, your level is stored only on your machine.
What data is shared with LinkedIn and JetBrains?
Your feature usage is tracked locally and isn’t shared with LinkedIn. After you connect, only your statement ID is sent when you reach a new level. The plugin doesn’t change your existing IDE data sharing settings, so no new data will be shared with JetBrains.
Do I need to keep the plugin installed after connecting?
Yes, if you want your progress to keep updating on LinkedIn. You can also share your level once and remove the plugin.
Can I connect multiple IDEs?
Yes. Each connected IDE gets its own statement on your profile.
Is the plugin free?
Yes, the plugin is free and works in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, Rider, GoLand, CLion, RustRover, and RubyMine, version 2025.3 or later. DataGrip isn’t supported. For the full list of level requirements, see the documentation.

posts.creator: Mark Downie
posts.title: Visual Studio November Update – Faster Workflows, Better Reviews
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Long waits have a way of breaking concentration. Visual Studio now does less repeated work when you open or close large solutions, launch designers and dialogs, and refresh source-control status. In Open Folder, you can also restore MSBuild dependencies without opening a solution first.
The new Copilot Chat is now on by default for eligible accounts. It handles long sessions more smoothly, accepts files dragged directly into a prompt, keeps conversations in their own tabs, and remembers your conversation mode and tool permissions for each session. Copilot also helps when it’s time to review: Change Groups organizes large pull requests into focused groups with summaries and review guidance, so you can see the structure before opening every file. In the CSS editor, color swatches show stylesheet colors as you edit. Get the Visual Studio 2026 Stable Channel and let us know where these changes help you most.
A More Responsive Visual Studio
Visual Studio now does less redundant work when large solutions load and close. Reusing project-directory information when refreshing C++ comment tasks reduced the measured Parse Solution phase by about 20% for Chromium and 9% for Unreal Engine in the PR’s test scenarios. These figures measure that phase only, not total solution-load time. Separately, Visual Studio removes an unused telemetry query during solution opening.
When you close a large solution, Visual Studio no longer rescans every open document for each project and cuts down on repeated file-watch cleanup. Solution Explorer source-control icon refreshes now run in bounded batches, giving the UI time to render in between. Legacy diagnostic providers also do less work when refreshing large Error List result sets.
When you open Add New Item, Visual Studio loads template registrations for the current project family first instead of initializing every registered project type. You keep the same template choices and project-switching behavior. Windows Forms and UWP XAML designers also avoid repeating some setup work. These changes target Windows Forms designer setup overhead, not your form’s initialization code, and UWP XAML designer startup, not every XAML project type.

Restore MSBuild Dependencies in Open Folder
Working from a folder doesn’t mean you have to open a solution before restoring dependencies. In Open Folder, right-click a supported solution or project file and select Restore to run the MSBuild Restore target through the existing folder build-action workflow.
If the project belongs to a discovered solution, Visual Studio keeps restore in that solution’s targeting context. The command doesn’t apply to CMake or other build providers, and it excludes C++ .vcxproj files.
Your browser does not support video playback.
A More Capable Copilot Chat
Copilot Chat in Visual Studio just got a new engine. Starting with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, it runs on the Microsoft Copilot SDK developed by GitHub, the same technology powering GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code. It’s on by default, and it’s a major upgrade: same models, more tasks solved, new ways to work.
Drag files from Solution Explorer or Windows File Explorer into Chat to attach them to a prompt instead of opening them in the editor. This also addresses a request for drag-and-drop file references. You can use the Test agent to generate tests when Copilot and its testing capability are enabled.
Your browser does not support video playback.
Choose Interactive for request-and-response work or Autopilot to let the agent continue until it considers the task complete. Set Manual or Allow all tool permissions independently. With Autopilot and Manual together, tools not configured for automatic approval are rejected instead of waiting for a prompt. Selecting Allow all shows a warning. Visual Studio saves these modes with each session, and Configure Defaults opens the related Chat settings. These controls address a request to retain MCP and mode settings.

The new engine also brings ways of working with Copilot that the previous experience didn’t offer.
Steer it mid-task. You no longer need to wait for Copilot to finish before redirecting it. Type a new instruction and press Enter, and Copilot applies it while it works. Until then, your message shows as Pending, and you can select the X to withdraw it.
See what Copilot actually did. Each step shows its results, not just the attempt. Expand any step to view the output, open it in the editor, or copy the exact command Copilot ran.
Review Pull Requests Faster with Change Groups
Large pull requests can mix features, tests, refactoring, and supporting changes across many files. Change Groups uses GitHub Copilot to organize related changes into focused review units, so you can understand the structure before opening every file.
Each group includes tags, a concise summary, and Review focus guidance. You can reorder groups, track progress across groups and files, move between comments, and review related files together instead of piecing them together from a flat list.
Your browser does not support video playback.
CSS Editing Improvements
Color swatches now appear beside CSS, SCSS, and LESS color values, making it easier to preview stylesheet colors in the editor. Swatches can resolve CSS custom properties, nested var() references and fallbacks, and resolvable SCSS and LESS variables. Select a swatch to see named-color suggestions or open the picker for hex and functional colors.

Updated schema data adds IntelliSense for modern CSS areas including anchor positioning, animations, fonts, masking, scroll animations, view transitions, and more. Media-query completion suggests feature names and values suited to each feature.
Your browser does not support video playback.

From our entire team, thank you for choosing Visual Studio! For the latest updates, resources, and news, check out the Visual Studio Hub and stay in touch.
Happy coding!
The Visual Studio team
